title: Poll: Dems open lead in two Ohio races
description: Former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, has an eight-point lead over U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican who was appointed by Gov. Mike DeWine, according to a poll of Ohio registered voters released last week. The same poll found that in the contest for governor, Democrat Amy Acton was up six points over Republican […]
text:
Former U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown, left, and U.S. Senator Jon Husted, right. (Photos from WEWS)Former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, has an eight-point lead over U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican who was appointed by Gov. Mike DeWine, according to a poll of Ohio registered voters released last week.
The same poll found that in the contest for governor, Democrat Amy Acton was up six points over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.
It was the first Ohio poll conducted by Marist University this cycle. 
It surveyed 1,298 registered voters between Sept. 24 and 27 using phone calls, text messages and the internet to solicit opinions. The margin of error was 3.8 percentage points.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Brown’s lead in the poll is significantly higher than the Real Clear Politics average of 3.7 points. The group’s average has Acton up by four points.
The Republican candidates are likely being dragged down by an unpopular president. The New York Times average places Donald Trump’s approval at 37%.
“Ohio registered voters approach the midterm election cycle with a sour mood toward President Donald Trump and lean Democratic in the state’s marquee contests,” a statement accompanying the Marist poll said.
The survey found that Trump is a little more popular with Ohioans — who gave him 42% approval — than with Americans as a whole.
The biggest share of Ohio voters, 41%, said their vote in the midterm election would be a vote against Trump. Thirty-three percent said Trump wasn’t much of a factor in their vote, and just 25% said they would vote in support of the president.
The same plurality, 41%, who said they plan their midterm votes as a statement against Trump, also said they’ve become economically worse off in the past year. Another 37% said their finances are about the same and just 19% said their finances have improved.
In addition to the economy, a quick, sharp backlash against data centers appears to be costing Ohio Republicans in terms of public opinion. In an August memo, the National Republican Senatorial Committee described how the backlash imperiled Husted’s chances — and those of future data centers.
“More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” it said. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”
The issue might help explain why, on the generic congressional ballot, Democrats have a three-point edge in Ohio. The Real Clear Politics puts the Democrats’ national lead on the generic congressional ballot at 8.5 points.
Election Day is Nov. 3. Military and overseas absentee voting start Thursday.
The deadline to register is Oct. 5. Early in-person and mail-in voting in Ohio start on Oct. 6.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Can Ohio do better than a gas tax suspension?
description: On Wednesday, the Ohio House of Representatives and the Ohio Senate approved a 90-day suspension of the state’s gas tax, planning to backfill it with funds from the state’s General Revenue fund. With a two-thirds majority in favor of the bill in each chamber, the bill will take effect immediately. The governor signed the measure […]
text:
A driver pumps gas at a Royal Farms in Columbia, Md., as rising fuel costs put pressure on household budgets nationwide. The national average price per gallon of regular gas is now $3.96, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. (Photos by Amanda Watford/Stateline)On Wednesday, the Ohio House of Representatives and the Ohio Senate approved a 90-day suspension of the state’s gas tax, planning to backfill it with funds from the state’s General Revenue fund. With a two-thirds majority in favor of the bill in each chamber, the bill will take effect immediately. The governor signed the measure into law Thursday.
The bill will cost the state an estimated $700 million according to the Legislative Service Commission. The bill itself sets aside $725 million in general revenue funds to cover these lost expenses.
While a majority of Ohio economists polled do not think a gas tax suspension will provide meaningful relief to Ohio households, this decision does reveal something: Ohio legislators are willing to pay $725 million to support households. What other ways could they do it?
Household rebate
One weakness of the current strategy is that a gas tax suspension only supports drivers. It is a mistake to say that the fuel price hike we have seen this year due to the War in Iran only impacts drivers. Fuel costs have driven up prices across the board and even households without cars are paying the price.
The current gas tax suspension disproportionately benefits two-car households and leaves Ohio’s 370,000 no-car households out, even as they face higher prices themselves. A change to a flat household rebate would mean each household would get about $150, with no-car households benefiting the same as 3+ car households.
Targeted rebate
This last point raises an important consideration: price increases are felt differently throughout the population. Low-income households are likely to feel the sting of higher prices harder than upper-income households. Targeting the rebate to the bottom quintile of households heaviest hit by increases would increase the per-household impact to $760.
Another option would be to target low-income households with children, the types of households that are likely to have the longest-lasting pain from economic shocks. Last year’s $450 million child tax credit proposal would provide up to $1,000 per household, providing more meaningful relief to more at-risk households at a much lower price than the gas tax proposal.
Targeted transportation relief
If lawmakers are particularly tied to transportation relief, there are ways to do that, too. County Job and Family Service offices already provide gas cards and bus passes to residents in need. Transit agencies like COTA have longstanding programs providing discounted transportation fares to people in need. Providing funds for county Job and Family Service offices and local transit agencies to temporarily expand transit options for low-income workers could concentrate relief in households most affected by rising transportation costs.
This time around, lawmakers opted for a simple, popular solution: temporarily suspend a gas tax to lead to a 90-day decrease in gas prices for every commuter, trucker, or nearby resident who fills up on gas in the state. Lawmakers showed they are willing to open their wallets in a moment like this. Next time Ohio residents experience a large, unexpected price shock they have the chance to be a little more creative and help people more at a lower price.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania is running out of power. Washington is part of the problem.
description: All too often these days, constructing a major energy infrastructure project in Pennsylvania involves years of court fights and permitting delays.
text:
All too often these days, constructing a major energy infrastructure project in Pennsylvania involves years of court fights and permitting delays. 
The PennEast Pipeline spent seven years in federal review and legal challenge only to be cancelled by its sponsors. Review for the Tioga Pathway Project, which broke ground this summer after a three-year approval process, was considered fast by current standards.
 In a state that is one of the world’s leading natural gas producers, this should not be the benchmark for efficiency. Time and again, Pennsylvanians have seen gigawatts of desperately needed energy infrastructure and electrical generation capacity lost to legal settlements rather than placed into service. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro has done his part in recent years to fix these issues at the state level. Now it is time for similar reforms federally.
Over the past several months, that dynamic has come into sharp focus. Since March 2026, the Trump Administration has reached agreements with several offshore wind developers to cancel their federal leases in exchange for a dollar-for-dollar reimbursement of the original lease amount. Six companies have collectively reallocated over $4 billion in planned wind capacity to redeploy into oil, gas, and LNG infrastructure.
The terms of those agreements have drawn criticism and legal scrutiny. Opponents have been quick to dismiss the deals as taxpayer-funded giveaways to the President’s allies at the expense of clean energy. 
Yet while the Trump Administration offers ample reason for ethical scrutiny, these reimbursements are neither a misuse of taxpayer money nor is it the first time the energy industry has battled executive whiplash. The reality is, unless Washington advances durable, bipartisan permitting reform, this broken cycle will keep repeating.
What’s most notable about the lease buy-back is the investment conditions that led the developers to walk away. Each of these companies acquired a lease through a competitive federal process and spent a significant amount of time and money working through established regulatory channels. 
They abandoned their projects for the same reason that the PennEast Pipeline folded and the Tioga Pathway Project barely skirted by: the policy environment is so uncertain that investors would rather cancel outright than gamble billions on developments in such an uncertain regulatory environment.
Unfortunately, these settlements also do nothing to address the conditions that produced them, nor do they resolve underlying concerns about grid reliability. The offshore wind cancellations are a visible and expensive illustration of what permitting dysfunction produces at scale. But the issues they faced are not unique are just one of many the obstacles developers of new electrical generation capacity face.
 PJM’s interconnection queue currently holds more than 90 gigawatts of generation capacity from a variety of energy sources waiting for a connection to the grid that the current permitting system cannot deliver on a predictable timeline. 
That backlog represents hundreds of billions in stranded investment. At the same time peak electricity demand is projected to grow by more than 30 gigawatts by 2030. The grid needs that capacity but the system tasked with approving it was not built for this moment.
 The National Environmental Policy Act – which requires federal agencies to evaluate the environmental impacts of major infrastructure projects before issuing a decision – is a big driver of these delays. The law served a legitimate purpose when it passed in 1970, but it has since enabled unworkable regulatory dysfunction. 
Average review timelines stretch past four years, environmental impact statements run hundreds of pages, and the constant threat of litigation means that projects completing federal review are simply entering the next phase of delay rather than the construction phase.
 Pennsylvania’s diverse energy economy depends on infrastructure that can be permitted and built within a timeframe that makes investment viable and leaves it uniquely exposed to this dysfunction. When that framework breaks down, it is the residents and business owners in the Commonwealth who absorb the consequences.  
Reforming the permitting process does not require gutting environmental reviews. It means setting timelines that agencies are required to meet, reducing the redundancy that builds up when multiple agencies analyze the same project in sequence, and providing enough legal predictability that investors can make long-term commitments without pricing in years of litigation risk.
Pennsylvania’s grid is under real pressure. What the Commonwealth needs now is Washington to follow the lead of Governor Shapiro and usher in a permitting system that allows new generation, of every kind, to reach the grid before the shortfall arrives.
 
T.J. Rooney previously served as chair of the Pennsylvania Democratic Party and is a former member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Is this what conservatism has come to?
description: Conservatives used to want to conserve. They wanted to conserve nature, wilderness, wildlife. They wanted to conserve art, historical sites, historical buildings, history itself. They valued American democracy, American traditions, and democratic institutions. Now they just want to destroy. The current administration leads this rage to destroy, tearing down[...]
text:
Kayakers on the Apalachicola River, via the Apalachicola Riverkeeper.Conservatives used to want to conserve.
They wanted to conserve nature, wilderness, wildlife.
They wanted to conserve art, historical sites, historical buildings, history itself.
They valued American democracy, American traditions, and democratic institutions.
Now they just want to destroy.
The current administration leads this rage to destroy, tearing down the East Wing of the White House, threatening the Kennedy Center with demolition, attacking museums, national parks and monuments — Trump has decimated Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, removing 90% of land owned by the American people, opening it  to mining and other commercial interests — and accelerating the climate crisis by repealing greenhouse gas standards and rolling back Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFÉ) standards.
The rule of law is under siege, with the administration ignoring court orders, flouting federal statutes, undermining the two other branches of government, and gleefully violating the Constitution.
Florida under Ron DeSantis is no different.
His administration refuses to protect historic buildings, natural treasures, and free thought, banning books, riding roughshod over civil rights, and doing their damnedest to impose right-wing juntas in our universities.
In 2024, the state bought The Gladstone, a Victorian house in Tallahassee.
Some of us were naive enough to hope they might restore the place or sell it to a group who could move it and save it.
The place was a fine example of the sharp-gabled, lacy woodwork style of the 1890s, the last of its kind along the capital’s main drag. It was pretty rickety, but not, according to historic preservationists, hopeless.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.But the DeSantis administration bulldozed it, claiming that because the property abutted the Governor’s Mansion grounds, it was a “security risk” and must be destroyed to expand the mansion’s perimeter and put in an all-important parking lot.
You’d almost think the state looks at anything beautiful, anything special, anything that contributes to our quality of life, and looks for a way to ruin it.
 ‘Golden era’?
DeSantis once boasted his first term was “a golden era for conservation,” vowing to eradicate the blue-green algae choking the life out of our lakes and rivers and setting up an initiative to save our reefs.
The reefs are breeding grounds and nurseries for 500 marine species and may be a source for new medicines. They protect coastal communities from beach erosion and storm surges and generate billions in recreation dollars.
Our waterways are still slimed with toxic algae and this year DeSantis cut all the funding from Florida’s Coral Reef Restoration and Recovery Initiative.
Why? Why not? The environment is clearly “woke.”
Remember when the governor insisted the now closed Alligator Alcatraz would do no damage to the Everglades?
That would be funny (almost) if it weren’t so false.
The facility’s 200 diesel generators belched out benzene and formaldehyde day and night, violating the Clean Air Act; its bright stadium lights, disrupting panther habitat, messing with the birds and amphibians who live in the ’glades, could be seen 18 miles away; its overflowing fuel trucks and port-a-potties leaked filth into the aquifer on which South Florida depends for drinking water.
The injuries inflicted weren’t only environmental.
Detainees were forced to live in unspeakably dirty conditions, denied food and medical care, denied access to lawyers, and were often placed in 4-foot by 4-foot outdoor metal cages, described by detention center staff as “calming areas” where inmates could have some “alone time,” and by Amnesty International as “torture.”
You know things were bad there when even the Department of Homeland Security, not known for its adherence to human rights, found the facility in violation of every possible standard.
Ron DeSantis blew the whole thing off. He didn’t know; the state wasn’t responsible; and what’s the big deal? It’s not like detainees are real people.
 ICE predations
Conservatives used to claim individual rights as an essential part of their philosophy. But here in Florida, rights only apply to state-approved citizens.
You can be locked up just because you don’t look sufficiently “American.”
Sometimes ICE rounds up undocumented people who have no right to be here.
Sometimes it detains people with pending citizenship applications or asylum claims, never mind they are in the country legally.
Sometimes it arrests American citizens.
This is hardly surprising in a country where ICE agents shoot protesters with impunity, where the highest court has gutted the Civil Rights Act, and the Trump administration threatens the coming elections.
What’s that old saying about the fish rotting from the head down?
 Dredge we must
The putrefaction from Washington has run downhill to Florida, where the Army Corps of Engineers wants to dredge the Apalachicola River.
Again.
In case you need reminding, this would be the same Corps responsible for the levees that collapsed in Hurricane Katrina, exacerbating death and destruction in New Orleans, and those disastrous discharges from Lake Okeechobee, polluting the Caloosahatchee and St. Lucie estuaries and killing Everglades flora and fauna.
The Corps is, of course, ultimately ruled by the geniuses at the Pentagon.
The Apalachicola River is one of the most biodiverse places on the planet, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, supporting hundreds of rare species of birds, fish, amphibians, and plants found almost nowhere else.
Nevertheless, the Corps is hell-bent on scraping out a navigational channel that its own reports show isn’t economically significant.
They’ll dig out the river bottom, endangered mollusks be damned, stacking the spoils in sand mounds which, in turn, choke the sloughs feeding the river, starving the floodplain forest and screwing up the delicate balance of salt and fresh water.
Thanks to DeSantis and the Legislature, local governments can no longer manage growth or protect water quality or sensitive lands or levy impact fees on developers to help with the cost of expanded infrastructure.
In 2025, the governor signed a law giving developers carte blanche.
Bulldoze those trees? Pollute that lake? Progress!
Citizens of Seminole and Orange County voted to preserve “rural boundaries,” designed to slow out-of-control growth and preserve habitat and forests. Florida legislators objected, squawking about “private property rights.”
If a developer objects to local tree ordinances or wetlands protections or impact fees or restrictions on the ungodly sprawl crawling across the state like kudzu on steroids, he is likely to prevail over the people who actually live in the place.
By now, you know the Trump administration and its DeSantis Mini-Me government want to tear down, chop down, and befoul. It seems to be in their DNA.
But some Democrats have caught the destruction disease as well.
Here in Tallahassee, run almost entirely by Democrats, the city allows — even encourages — what they call “growth” and many of those of us who live here call “unsustainable sprawl.”
When some rapacious developer cuts a bunch of old trees — the kind that take a century or more to mature — without permission, he gets a slap on the wrist from city or county government, maybe a small fine.
The rapacious developer shrugs: It’s the cost of doing business.
 ‘Paused’
Welaunee, 6,600 acres in northeast Leon County, is slated to become one of those “master-planned communities” of the sort defacing Florida south of the Suwannee River.
The development has been “paused,” supposedly so citizens can express concerns and ask questions, but if anyone thinks it can be stopped altogether, well, they don’t realize Florida’s most important relationship is not with democracy or nature, it’s with money.
The company wants to build 6,591 houses and create 425,000 square feet of “retail space” (probably called “shoppes”) and multi-lane roads.
One section has already been completed, a “community” called Canopy — though it has no canopy, barely any trees — largely rows of beige houses that could be anywhere: the Atlanta suburbs, the outskirts of Orlando, the gated cookie-cutter villages along I-75.
If Canopy is anything to go by, Welaunee will be an abomination.
The wetlands, the cherished green spaces, the old-growth oaks, the lakes and streams, the wildlife habitat, the peace and quiet, the beauty we should cherish — and conserve — all gone.
It will be a miracle if in 10 years the whole state isn’t one big expanse of concrete and asphalt, an endless subdivision punctuated here and there by data centers, Wawas, and strip malls.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A renewed plea to safeguard SNAP in the Farm Bill
description: Building a just food system requires community-rooted partnerships capable of system-wide thinking
text:
In June of 2025 we co-authored A plea to safeguard SNAP  urging lawmakers to protect the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) as federal reconciliation debates threatened eligibility rules and state funding. That proposal was signed into law as H.R. 1 (the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”) on July 4, 2025. The legislation imposed stricter work requirements, shortened benefit durations, shifted administrative costs onto state budgets, and cut federal aid from our local economies, directly impacting local grocery stores and farm stands.
SNAP is the nation’s most effective food security safety-net and is therefore invaluable to the health and well-being of society, including state economies. Since the implementation of H.R. 1, we have heard repeatedly from leaders at Connecticut food banks and pantries that the charitable food system is stretched thin and cannot shoulder unprecedented hunger alone. This sentiment comes amid additional cuts to proven federal programs that not only work, but actively transform a fraught system, such as the Local Food Purchase Assistance Cooperative Agreement Program (LFPA, or Farm to Pantry) and the Local Food for Schools Cooperative Agreement Program (LFSP, or Farm to School).
Food Insecurity in Connecticut 
Connecticut holds the highest rate of food insecurity in New England, at an estimated 16%. Additionally, 40% of Connecticut households fall into the ALICE category (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed). These are working families who earn above the federal poverty limit, yet consistently lack sufficient income to afford basic necessities like fresh food. Standard SNAP income caps (typically 130% of the federal poverty level, expanded to 200% in certain states) fail to capture the millions living paycheck-to-paycheck in this demographic. When policy ignores ALICE families, hunger grows exponentially.
Food and farming systems do not exist in a vacuum. While structural, geographic, and transportation obstacles prevent low-income households from accessing nutrient-dense foods, there are other contributing factors such as geopolitical instability, tariffs, climate disruptions, and extreme corporate consolidation that allow major food conglomerates to keep grocery prices artificially high. All of these converging pressures make the cuts to SNAP not only immoral, but a major driver of the food insecurity crisis.
In short, three primary policy-influenced decisions are inflicting hunger on our communities: persistent barriers to access, soaring food prices, and deep SNAP cuts.
The Farm Bill
The Farm Bill is one of the most consequential pieces of federal legislation in our nation. It determines how the federal government supports everything from agricultural subsidies, crop insurance, farm loans, conservation programs, to local and regional food systems. The Farm Bill is designed to encourage compromise between the needs of farmers and the need for affordable food. Its largest component, Title IV, oversees Nutrition and SNAP.
Earlier this month, the Farm Bill was voted out of the Senate Agriculture Committee and is expected to be brought to the Senate floor in the coming weeks before returning to the House. 
The debate between legislators falls along party lines over the future of federal nutrition funding and who should bear its cost. Federal food assistance isn’t just a relief program; it directly drives economic activity for local farms and vendors. Lawmakers must not balance the federal budget at the expense of thriving communities. 
The Senate’s current impasse on the Farm Bill gives us an opportunity to choose a better path. Achieving lasting food security requires two simultaneous actions: safeguarding federal nutrition benefits and investing heavily in localizing food and agricultural infrastructure. 
As the National Young Farmers Coalition points out, “For our farmers, these 4.7 million people forced off of the program represent a massive loss of purchasing power in the very communities they serve. When families are “kicked out” of SNAP, they lose the ability to shop at farmers’ markets and farm stands, effectively shutting down local market channels that young farmers rely on to remain viable. A Farm Bill that does not restore these nutrition investments fails to reinforce the foundation of our agricultural system, leaving both vulnerable families and the next generation of farmers at risk.”
Power in Local Systems and Trusted Partnerships
Connecticut is home to 5,000 mostly small, diversified farms powering a $4 billion agricultural sector. Strengthening farm viability directly strengthens community food access. We must commit catalytic public and private investment in farmland preservation and local and regional supply chains, such as food hubs, while expanding farm-to-institution initiatives, supporting diverse farmers, increasing farmland access, and doubling SNAP incentives at local markets. Building a just food system requires community-rooted partnerships capable of system-wide thinking. No single entity can resolve food insecurity in isolation.
We call on our community to champion access to fresh, local food as a fundamental human right, and to demand our Senators pass a Farm Bill that reverses the damaging SNAP cuts under H.R. 1. Take action here.
Ali Ghiorse is executive director of The Foodshed Network and Karen Saggese is site director of Food Rescue US – Fairfield County. They are co-leaders of Greenwich Foodshed Alliance.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Sen. John Kennedy’s possible presidential run depends on ‘a bunch of goobers’
description: Sen. John Kennedy appeared on NBC’s “Meet the Press” where host Kristen Welker asked him outright if he would run for president.
text:
U.S. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, delivered a speech at the Iowa Faith and Freedom Coalition fall fundraiser Sep. 19, 2026 at the Airport Holiday Inn in Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Louisiana’s loquacious junior U.S. senator said Sunday he will ponder a run for president depending on which of his fellow Republicans pursues the office in 2028.
Sen. John Kennedy appeared on NBC’s “Meet the Press” where host Kristen Welker asked him outright if he would run for president. Kennedy said his current intention is to seek re-election in two years, but he added that he would consider a presidential run if he believes he could no longer be effective in Congress.
“What’s the old Judds’ song? ‘Why not me on a rainy day? Why not me to love your blues away?’” Kennedy said.
He added that while he hasn’t made a decision on the presidential race, he will keep track of what other GOP members emerge as candidates.

“On my side of the aisle, if a bunch of goobers run … and one of the goobers might win, and I think I can do a better job, I would consider running,” Kennedy said. “But right now, I’m running for re-election.”



Kennedy has held his U.S. Senate seat since 2017. He will become Louisiana’s senior senator once Sen. Bill Cassidy, who lost the Republican primary to Congresswoman Julia Letlow in May, leaves office in January.  
When Welker asked Kennedy about the possibility of running against Vice President JD Vance, the senator declined to respond directly. 
“I’m not going to talk about another potential candidate. I’m just not there yet,” he said.
If Kennedy, who turns 75 next month, were to run for president and win, he would become the third oldest person to enter the office behind President Donald Trump and Joe Biden.
Kennedy has spent the past month traveling to campaign on behalf of other Republican incumbents and candidates running for Congress. Those trips have taken him to states likely to be battlegrounds in the 2028 election, and Kennedy said he will continue to stump for the GOP on his volition.
“I’m gonna go wherever my political people tell me to go,” he said. “I have my own political operation. I don’t take orders from my leadership. I do it my way.” 
Kennedy was also asked to comment about a recent social media post from the president in which he gave out the cellphone number of U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Arkansas, who voted against a measure Trump backed to eliminate daylight saving time.
“The president, as we know, can be sometimes … he exists loudly. He can be tempestuous. He can go from zero to a-hole in about 3 seconds,” Kennedy said. “I don’t think he should have given out Tom’s cell phone number.”
Rahm Emanuel, former Chicago mayor and White House chief of staff for President Barack Obama, appeared on “Meet the Press” before the segment with Kennedy, who predicted Emanuel will seek the Democratic nomination for president in 2028. 
Emanuel, who was in Louisiana last week to learn about post-pandemic K-12 education progress, has said he is considering a run but has not taken official steps to launch a candidacy.    
“Rahm has a big brain. He has big ideas,” Kennedy told Welker. “What I appreciate about him is that while many members of his party want to sit around and debate whether a man can breastfeed, Rahm wants to talk about important things.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Inmates moving to new Rapid City women’s prison, but dilapidated unit in Pierre remains in use
description: South Dakota’s recently opened women’s prison in Rapid City held 79 women at the end of September, the first month the state began to move them there from the women’s prison campus in Pierre.  Overcrowding in the buildings at the older women’s prison spurred the construction of the $87 million Rapid City complex. For years, […]
text:
Vehicles fill the parking lot of South Dakota's Rapid City Correctional Facility, a women's prison, on Oct. 1, 2026. The complex includes multiple additional structures behind the main building. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s recently opened women’s prison in Rapid City held 79 women at the end of September, the first month the state began to move them there from the women’s prison campus in Pierre. 
Overcrowding in the buildings at the older women’s prison spurred the construction of the $87 million Rapid City complex. For years, the state has paid Hughes County to house some female state prison inmates at the jail in Pierre and held hundreds of women in a minimum security unit that state engineers have deemed unfit for human habitation.
The new women’s prison on the state’s western side has 288 beds. In addition to standard housing units, the campus has facilities for chemical dependency treatment and for a mother-baby program that lets qualifying women live in a home-like environment with their newborn children.
Department of Corrections spokesperson Michael Winder said its population of 79 will grow as its operations ramp up. 
On July 10, the date of a ribbon cutting for the prison, Winder told South Dakota Searchlight that inmates would start to move in “beginning next month,” but the first inmates didn’t arrive until September.

As of Thursday, 466 women remained in prison custody in secure facilities Pierre, Winder said in an email. There were 64 held off-site at the Hughes County Jail and 208 in the minimum security unit, with the remaining people in secure detention housed in the main prison unit. 
Beyond the women in secure facilities, the total population of women in state prison custody includes some who live in community facilities, such as halfway houses. 
Corrections Secretary Nick Lamb told lawmakers in February that the minimum unit is “not suited for occupancy,” according to multiple assessments across multiple years, and has “structural deficiencies.”
Lamb’s remarks came in support of a bill to set aside $682,825 to demolish the building, which lawmakers passed and Gov. Larry Rhoden signed into law.
All maintenance work on the building ceased once lawmakers approved funding for the new Rapid City prison in 2023, Lamb said in February, and the demolition would be needed because the building will “continue to degrade and pose life safety concerns.”
The women in the minimum unit would be transferred to Rapid City “later this summer,” Lamb told lawmakers. 
Winder told South Dakota Searchlight that “there have been no substantial maintenance projects” at the minimum unit since Lamb said that.
The number of South Dakotans in prison systemwide has risen by hundreds since spring. A policy change announced this spring by Gov. Larry Rhoden makes it easier to bring paroled inmates back to prison for breaking the rules of their supervision agreements after early release. The number of parolees in custody spiked shortly after the announcement.
Inmates are also being denied early release at a higher rate.
In February, the total inmate population was 3,720. Of those, 580 were women.
At the end of August — the most recent population count available when this story was published — there were 4,049 inmates in custody. Of those, 632 were women. There were eight more women in the minimum unit on Aug. 31 than there are today. 
In response to a question about whether the minimum unit in Pierre would remain in service now that the Rapid City facility is open, Winder said the Department of Corrections intends to demolish the building in accordance with the Legislature’s decision.
The timeline for removal is not set, however, and will take place when the unit “is no longer needed,” Winder said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont needs fewer small towns and some taller buildings
description:
Rural life is holding Vermont back, and the fix is closing the countryside.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont needs fewer small towns and some taller buildings.
text:
Dear Editor,
As VTDigger’s recent reporting clearly indicates, over its last several sessions, the Vermont Legislature has danced around the predominant and defining cause of Vermont’s historic dilemma. Our lawmakers lack the courage to tackle this reality with the bold, decisive steps that a forthright statement of the problem requires. Absent the necessary clarity of definition, half-measures and inadequate solutions dominate their discussions, and the long-suffering people of Vermont fail to find the respite they deserve.
In two words, the words the Legislature is clearly too craven to admit, Vermont suffers from excessive ruralization. People in Vermont are simply far too few and way too spread out, and as a result, Vermont is the very definition of inefficiency. Schools are too small, neighbors are forced to depend on the generosity of friends for basic social interactions, healthcare is monstrously expensive, the aging rely on the care of their families, and public transportation is woefully inadequate. 

READ MORE

The rest of the world figured out eons ago that efficient human life takes place in urban centers dominated by high-rise buildings, proximity to social services, concentrated economic endeavors and cultural opportunities. Life in the sticks forces individuals to fend for themselves, make do with limited resources and improvise Band-Aid solutions. Why would a sane person choose to live that way? But our Legislature continues ignoring the real problem. Obviously, Vermont needs to close the countryside, expand its current two or three metropolitan areas and create genuine cosmopolitan life for Vermont’s beleaguered rustics. 
With a few precise strokes of its legislative pen, Montpelier could create the genuine disincentives necessary to shut down the wasteful boonies, expand essential construction and business optimism, and create real cities instead of the half-populated hamlets now pretending to urban life. Construct a few 40- or 50-story buildings in Burlington and Brattleboro, create sufficient metropolitan population to build efficient schools, consolidate inefficient family farms, shutter tiny villages and close nasty dirt roads, and we could begin turning this podunk state around.   
Free our people from the demands of country living. Provide real cities. With proper legislative attention, the trials of hick-ville Vermont can soon be a backwoods of the past. Wake up, legislators, and bring Vermont into the 21st century.  
Jay Stroud 
Quechee, Vt.

description: The Cape Henlopen Vikings (4-0) defeated the Hodgson Silver Eagles (1-4), 35-28, on October 3 to remain undefeated to start the season. The Vikings are 4-0 for the first time in over a decade.   MIDDLETOWN, DE — Normally when Cape Henlopen senior Jameson Tingle is mentioned in correlation to a football game it’s because of his talents on the ... Read More
text:
Cape Henlopen senior Jameson Tingle recovers a fumble for the Vikings in their win over Hodgson. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
The Cape Henlopen Vikings (4-0) defeated the Hodgson Silver Eagles (1-4), 35-28, on October 3 to remain undefeated to start the season. The Vikings are 4-0 for the first time in over a decade.
 
MIDDLETOWN, DE — Normally when Cape Henlopen senior Jameson Tingle is mentioned in correlation to a football game it’s because of his talents on the offensive side of the ball. On a rainy Saturday afternoon, Tingle’s impact on defense was what earned Cape Henlopen its fourth win of the season and first 4-0 start in 12 years.
The Silver Eagles trailed the Vikings by seven when their final drive of the game started on their own three-yard line with a little over eight minutes remaining in the game. Hodgson quarterback, senior Kevin Browning, connected with fellow senior Dorian Wilson on a 31-yard pass and subsequent runs from Browning brought Hodgson into Cape Henlopen territory. The Silver Eagles drove the ball to the Viking 18-yard line, needing inches to extend the drive on fourth and less than a yard.
Browning rushed the ball into the middle of the Cape Henlopen defense and was met by Viking junior Geoffrey Davis rushing in from his spot in the secondary to make the tackle. Davis’ tackle hit the arm of Browning and jarred the ball loose. Tingle quickly jumped on the ball securing possession for the Viking offense with 1:25 left to play.
“Coach just called a blitz on my part so I was already in the mix,” Tingle said postgame. “I seen my teammate knock the ball out and after I see that it’s just look around and try to find the ball and then I found it and I dove. I could’ve been scared, I could’ve did this, but I didn’t really care. I see ball, get ball, and luckily I was able to get it.”  
Tingle’s defensive play completed a strong second half for the University of Delaware commit as he led the Vikings to a comeback victory. 
The Silver Eagles started the game with a recovery on an onside kick and turned the possession into eight points on the game’s first drive. Senior running back, Keytwan Sabur, scored the touchdown on a 23-yard run and scored Hodgson’s second touchdown on its next drive via a four yard run. The Vikings answered the pair of touchdowns with a couple short yardage touchdown runs from Tingle, tying the game, 14-14, forty seconds into the second quarter.
Hodgson senior Keytwan Sabur runs the ball for the Silver Eagles. Sabur scored Hodgson’s first two touchdowns. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
Hodgson fired right back with its senior signal caller on a 14-play drive that ended with a one-yard Browning touchdown and a completed two-point conversion pass from Browning to sophomore Julian Coleman. Tingle and senior Aidan Lehmuth connected on a 26-yard catch and score, but the two-point try was no good, leaving Hodgson in the lead, 22-20. Browning completed the first half scoring with his second rushing touchdown, putting the Silver Eagles ahead, 28-20.
That’s when the quarterback Cape Henlopen senior Stephen Sivels nicknamed “Thanos” took over.
“I call him Thanos [because] he do it all [on] both sides of the field,” Sivels said about Tingle. “He got a fumble recovery, passing touchdowns, punching it in, all that so I call him Thanos.”  
Tingle completed eight of ten pass attempts in the second half for 168 passing yards and a touchdown. Tingle’s passing touchdown was a 46-yard catch and run to Sivels that tied the score after a run from Tingle on the two-point conversion. Sivels’ touchdown grab was one of five catches he hauled in throughout the game. Sivels ended the game with over 100 receiving yards. 
“Jameson, he’s a great quarterback. He can swing it from the opposite side and hit me right on the spot, so yeah, I really love playing with Jameson because he’s a really good quarterback,” Sivels said.
Tingle makes a leaping throw to a receiver down field. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
Tingle scored the go-ahead touchdown on a three-yard rush with a little over eight minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. It was the first time Cape Henlopen led during the afternoon. Tingle finished the game with 295 passing yards, 109 rushing yards and five total touchdowns. 
“Just my teammates man. It’s just what we’ve been through, summers since we’ve been young, I’ve been playing with these guys for a long time, so they’re able to give me the courage, be able to keep me level-headed and yeah they just give me the courage to do everything,” Tingle said about how he’s able to stay composed in adverse game situations. “All kudos to them.”  
Cape Henlopen’s next game is a homecoming matchup against Appoquinimink on October 9. The game will be played in Lewes, Delaware, and start at 7:00 p.m. 
The Silver Eagles next game will be against St. Georges on Friday, October 9, at 3:45 p.m. St. Georges has won the matchup two years in a row.

name: VTDigger
title: Wood banks prep for long winter months
description:
The United Way of Lamoille County is among the organizations helping Vermonters gear up for winter and heating their homes with wood.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Wood banks prep for long winter months.
text:
Students help load wood onto a truck to be delivered to families in need in the area. Photo by Gordon Miller/News & Citizen

This story by Liberty Darr and Patrick Bilow was first published in the News & Citizen on Sept. 17, 2026. 
One in three Vermonters will heat their homes with wood this winter, but as the cost and difficulty of sourcing wood increases for some, a handful of local organizations are providing free cords to those in need.
Recently volunteers donned safety gloves and earmuffs for an annual firewood workday in Morristown with United Way of Lamoille County. Wood splitters of various shapes and sizes fired on all cylinders as volunteers chucked chunks of wood into trucks for home deliveries.
The United Way’s firewood program is one of multiple wood banks in the Lamoille County area that provide free firewood to local seniors, veterans and income-eligible families to help keep their homes warm throughout the winter.
According to the most recent statistics from the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation, as of 2019, just over a third of Vermont households use cordwood as a heating source — a statistic that is largely unchanged from reported usage in the 2014-2015 heating season and similar to usage in the 1990s.
Meanwhile, nearly two-thirds of Vermont households using cordwood rely on it as their primary source of heat, while just over one-third use it for supplemental heat, according to the department’s 2019 Residential Fuel Assessment.
The survey also indicates that Vermont households burned more than 400,000 estimated cords of wood during the 2018-2019 heating season — 18% higher than the estimated total number burned during the 2014-2015 season and higher than any previously reported estimate since 1986.
As reliance on wood as a heat source increased marginally in Vermont as of 2019, the price of a cord skyrocketed to around $500, according to those familiar with the industry. Meanwhile, recent increases in oil prices anecdotally pushed some Vermonters back to burning wood.
While financial assistance is often provided for oil burners, less is available for wood burners. According to information from the state’s Department for Children and Families from 2023, just under 2,000 households that heat with wood and pellets were issued benefits.
That’s where wood banks are stepping up.
Keeping neighbors warm
Not only can burning wood be cost intensive, but it’s also labor intensive, creating a relatively substantial barrier to the heat source, especially for older demographics.
“If you’re elderly but you have a wood stove and can’t afford to replace it, then you’re going to end up needing firewood, and it can be really cumbersome or impossible for folks to process their own wood,” said Clarissa French, executive director of United Way of Lamoille County.
In any given year, the organization gives away between 40 and 65 cords, based on demand, which some providers say is increasing. Most of the wood is harvested on state land and donated by the state of Vermont through its Wood Warms program.
Stephanie Ferro, a United Way board member, and her husband, Bryan, operate their own wood bank in Stowe called Vermont Warm Hearts, which he launched as a high school student in Woodstock.
Between Lamoille and Windsor counties, the organization delivered emergency wood to nearly 20 families last year.
They are often contacted during emergency situations when a family is almost out of wood in the dead of winter. The small, family-run operation — their daughter Sophia is involved — tries to fulfill those deliveries within 24 hours.
“The demand is going up,” Stephanie Ferro said, adding that there is a substantial group of people in need that are just above the income threshold the state utilizes for determining eligibility for fuel assistance.
They are often left to choose between feeding their families or heating their homes, she said.
A wider reach
Another wood provider, Wood4Good, is expanding its influence in Lamoille County. Since launching in 2019, the nonprofit has donated and delivered approximately 50 cords of wood each year to towns across Vermont.
Eric Axelrod started Wood4Good with his son after a pile of firewood in their yard had grown too large to continue storing. They gave a few cords away and have been chasing that feeling ever since.
“We gave that wood away, and the family we gave it to said to us, ‘This is the first winter we’re going to be OK,’” Axelrod said. “Then we found another family that was burning furniture to keep their home warm.”
After years of increased reliance on its service, Wood4Good recently expanded its influence in Lamoille County. The nonprofit processes firewood with automated splitters in Jericho but has storage facilities throughout the state, including in Johnson.
The Wolcott Selectboard is also mulling whether to allow Wood4Good to clear trees in the town’s newly established forest as it expands municipal wastewater services and expands trail networks on the land.
Several towns in Chittenden County, including Hinesburg and Shelburne, allocate funds for the nonprofit. No towns in Lamoille County have yet to follow suit.
As winter sets in and households scramble for firewood, Axelrod agreed with other wood banks that need is increasing and recently spiked. Just this year, he received 50 new applications for firewood next winter.
Recently he also received a letter from an elderly customer who said she and her dog almost froze to death last winter huddling under an electric blanket.
“That’s the story of a lot of Vermont. That story is very, very real,” Axelrod said.
One for all
These three wood banks — United Way, Vermont Warm Hearts and Wood4Good — do not operate in silos.
To create the greatest impact, French from United Way said, local wood banks are trying to network more and regularly attend collaborative meetings with state officials.
“There’s not enough wood bank activity in the state, but there are little wood banks trying to make an impact all over the place,” she said.
For example, Stephanie Ferro does a lot of coordinating between her family’s organization and United Way. If the call is one that doesn’t fit the bill for Vermont Warm Hearts, they may relay the request to another organization. Her and her husband’s organization provides emergency support, whereas United Way doesn’t typically.
“When we moved here, and I heard what United Way was doing, I said to my husband, ‘I want to get involved and let’s see if we can work together so that we can share resources, share brain power and share energy,’ and I think it’s definitely working for us,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: After a costly dry spell, a wetter outlook
description:
Dartmouth research found that drought has become less frequent and less intense across the Northeast, which could help inform Vermont’s future disaster preparation.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After a costly dry spell, a wetter outlook.
text:
People walk along the beach at St. Albans Bay in September 2025. The 2025 drought brought water levels on Lake Champlain to near record lows. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Droughts like the one that cost Vermont farmers nearly $16 million last year might be becoming less common, a new Dartmouth College study suggests, as increased rainfall makes dry spells less frequent and less intense across the Northeast.
But farmers shouldn’t pack up their irrigation equipment just yet.
“What this study does not tell you is that there will not be drought in the Northeast,” said lead author Jonathan Winter. “That is not the case. We have always had drought, and we will continue to have drought.”
The study, published Thursday in the Journal of Hydrometeorology, found that drought in the Northeast has been 59% less frequent and 19% less intense since the mid-1980s compared with the entire period from 1901 to 1983. Winter and his team used more than a century of weather station records to calculate a drought index for the region.
The findings could help Vermont decide how to prepare for drought alongside other weather threats.
Relatively little peer-reviewed research has examined these regional drought trends, which means this study can contribute to a greater understanding of them, Winter said.
Last year’s agricultural losses illustrate how damaging an individual drought can be despite the long-term regional decline. Vermont farmers lost nearly $16 million in drought-related damage last year.
The Vermont Economic Development Authority, which assists businesses affected by disasters, offered loans to those affected. Lawmakers also passed Act 78, establishing a permanent fund for farmers and foresters facing financial losses from weather events.
Supply and demand
The study’s relatively simple drought metric helps describe broad trends, but Vermont State climatologist Lesley-Ann Dupigny-Giroux said drought and its effects are more complicated. She has studied drought and extreme weather in Vermont since the late 1990s.
Drought, in the simplest terms, is a shortage of precipitation. But, its intensity and impact can be affected by many factors, including geography, season, temperature and the type of precipitation.
 “As long as you have a greater demand (on water) than you have supply, you’re in a drought,” she said. “This is exacerbated by how ‘thirsty’ the air or ground is at the time.”
A ‘thirsty’ atmosphere, for example, can evaporate moisture from the ground and worsen drought conditions.
Dupigny-Giroux said new types of drought have emerged in the past decade. These include flash droughts, which intensify quickly, and ecological droughts, the effects of which can actually alter ecosystems.
Vermont was more drought-prone but began getting wetter around the 1970s, Dupigny-Giroux said. That’s about a decade before the shift identified in Winter’s regional research. She attributed Vermont’s change to a combination of factors, including a warmer atmosphere and a shift in storm tracks over the region.
In fact, drought conditions preceded some of Vermont’s worst floods, Dupigny-Giroux said. She pointed to the drought and flood of 1927 and a short period of drought conditions before Irene hit in 2011. There was also a drought in the spring and early summer in 2023 leading up to the historic floods in July, she said.
“By always keeping an eye on history is what allows you to say Vermont is a state that goes from droughts to floods in the blink of an eye,” Dupigny-Giroux said.
The Northeast’s drought decline contrasts with conditions elsewhere in the country. More than half of the U.S. experienced drought conditions this past spring, while the West has endured a prolonged megadrought described in research published in Nature Climate Change as the driest conditions in at least 1,200 years.
Weather disasters strain state and local resources, complicating decisions about which risks to prepare for and how to spend limited funds. Winter said he hopes the findings can help guide those decisions.
“To the extent that we can deploy awareness of, as well as preparedness and adaptation strategies to cope with droughts, these would help move us towards a more resilient place than waiting for droughts to occur and reacting to them,” Dupigny-Giroux said.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont officials and advocates tackle voting accessibility concerns ahead of November election
description:
Data shows low voter turnout for disabled in Vermont; efforts afoot to change that.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont officials and advocates tackle voting accessibility concerns ahead of November election.
text:
A voter carries ballots past a booth in Shelburne on Primary Day, Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Voter rights advocates are pushing on several fronts to ensure voting access for Vermonters ahead of the general election in November.
The Secretary of State’s office launched a voter accessibility task force in coalition with advocacy groups last year that focused on expanding resources for people with disabilities, people experiencing homelessness, survivors of domestic and sexual violence and people who are incarcerated. 
Nursing home residents were also identified as a group with voter accessibility needs, said Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas. Nursing home groups have already been working to meet those needs, including guidance in September from the Vermont Health Care Association.
The guidance is aimed at providing clarity on federal and state regulations relating to residents’ rights and the voting assistance process in nursing homes in Vermont.
“I hope that the guidance that we created will help people be more confident in and more willing to assist people who need assistance in exercising their right to vote,” Kaili Kuiper, state long-term care ombudsman with Vermont Legal Aid, said, who provided input on the guidance.
The effort followed a Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services memo in July, reminding nursing facilities and staff that they must avoid inference, coercion or influencing residents while preserving and promoting the right to vote for residents. 
The memo was issued after a social worker was charged with election fraud in Texas for unlawfully registering residents to vote and an investigation by law enforcement officials in Wisconsin into allegations that eight people “whose mental capacities had diminished due to age or disease” voted. The guidance only reinforces existing law and is not a change in regulations. 
Kuiper said that she worried that the memo would cause a “chilling effect.” 
“I was afraid that facilities might take from that that anyone who has any sign of cognitive impairment shouldn’t be assisted with voting, or even shouldn’t be allowed to vote,” Kuiper said.
That concern was echoed by Copeland Hanzas who reiterated that Vermont state law prescribes that every Vermonter should have access to their ballot and should be able to ask someone for assistance in filling out their ballot. 
Voting in nursing homes is driven by resident choice, and staff should let residents know that elections are coming up and what their voting options are, Helen Labun, executive director of the Vermont Health Care Association, said. She added that residents should be asked whether they want to vote and if they would like help. 
Vermont law prohibits voting if an individual is ruled incompetent by a judge, according to the guidance. Facilities should provide assistance to any resident who is able to indicate their voting choice, the guidance says. 
Nursing home staff should document residents’ permission for assistance in the voting process  and individuals cannot deliver more than 25 mail-in ballots from residents without a justice of the peace in attendance, according to the guidance. 
While some advocates are worried the memo could affect the voting rights of nursing home residents, the voting process is much the same as it has been for past elections at the Vermont Veterans Home in Bennington, said Melissa Jackson, CEO of the facility. 
Staff meet with veterans living at the facility to determine whether they would like to vote and organize transportation to the polls. Oliver Allen, a veteran living at the facility, has played a role in sharing nonpartisan voter information with residents and encouraging them to vote. 
Allen says he tells residents, “You can’t serve your country anymore in uniform, but you can get out to the voting booths and cast your ballot.”
Vermont ranks low in voting access for people with disabilities, according to a 2024 MIT analysis of U.S. Census data, which found a lower turnout rate for people who reported having a disability compared to those who reported no disability.
Barriers facing people with disabilities voting in Vermont include a lack of accessible voter information for people with visual or cognitive disabilities or limited English proficiencies, and a lack of transportation options for people with disabilities who want to vote in-person, according to a Disability Rights Vermont report. 
Vermont likely also ranks low compared to other states because municipal and school elections sometimes are held in buildings that are not handicapped-accessible, Copeland Hanzas said, and local communities in Vermont often lack the funds to upgrade buildings with ramps and elevators or find another location for Town Meeting Day.
Copeland Hanzas said she has a longer-term goal of piloting an electronic voting system for municipal elections that would allow voters to make voting decisions securely by phone if they cannot gather in a physical space. This would open up the local democratic process to more people, said Copeland Hanzas, but would require legislative action and a statutory change. 
Copeland Hanzas also wants to ensure Vermonters are aware of the accessible voting tablet-based system that allows people with disabilities to vote in private in every polling place in the state, which was first rolled out in 2018. 
Survivors of domestic and sexual violence also can face unique barriers to voting, including safety concerns, residential address confidentiality and housing instability, and a newly developed voter guide helps people navigate these challenges, said Charlie Parker Gliserman, policy director with the Vermont Network Against Domestic and Sexual Violence, which serves on the task force. 
Copeland Hanzas said the taskforce is also working to ensure people experiencing homelessness know they can register to vote using the address of a shelter or other location where they are residing.
The Secretary of State’s Office is working with the Department of Corrections to ensure mail-in ballots are forwarded to people who are incarcerated, and that they have access to a voter guide the Secretary of State’s Office is developing, which will be mailed to every household in Vermont. 
Copeland-Hanzas encouraged anyone who sees any irregularities in the election process to report it to a municipal clerk, the Secretary of State or the Attorney General for investigation. 
“Vermonters should be confident that our town and city clerks are running clean and fair and accessible elections in our communities,” Copeland-Hanzas said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Artificial intelligence in the classroom
authors: Josh Aubol, Steve Stein, Peter Klosterman
description: A considered approach to AI is necessary if we want teachers to make classroom-level decision rooted in student learning, three Central Washington University experts say.
text:
A considered approach to AI remains necessary if we want teachers to make classroom-level decision rooted in student learning, three experts argue.(Photo by Maskot/Getty Images)As the debate about the role of artificial intelligence carries on, teachers once again find themselves at the forefront of a discussion about the impact of new technologies on education. For many teachers, the outlook isn’t great.
As one teacher wrote in a recent survey we conducted, “I don’t know whether teachers or students will be relevant in the future.”
Yet not all teachers’ attitudes towards AI are so bleak, and there may be some evidence as to what can help teachers use these tools in a way that centers student learning.
In May of this year, as faculty members working with Central Washington University’s College in the High School program, we surveyed 222 high school math and English teachers. The survey asked teachers a variety of questions about their attitudes toward AI, institutional policies, professional development opportunities, their own AI use, and student AI use.
Teachers reported significant differences in their attitude towards teaching since AI has appeared depending on academic discipline; 57.0% of English teachers reported that their overall attitude towards teaching has worsened since AI appeared, while only 37.6% of math teachers reported a similar change in attitude.
As AI use in schools grows, lawmakers and districts scramble to set up guardrails

The difference between the two disciplines was even larger when it came to concerns about academic integrity, with 83.7% of English teachers reporting academic integrity concerns, and only 54.9% of math teachers reporting the same concerns.
Yet despite a worsening attitude towards teaching and concerns about academic integrity, English teachers also reported greater confidence teaching students to use AI responsibly (45.5% for English and 24.4% for math) and were more likely to require students to experiment with AI in their classes (34.1% for English and 14.6% for mMath).
Although this increased confidence seems contradictory at first, it may reflect the type of AI tools teachers and students have at their disposal. Large language models, which produce convincing (if sometimes factually inaccurate) writing as their output, are often reported to make frequent mistakes when completing simple mathematical calculations.
Because of this, the difference between English and math may reflect the tools themselves, rather than any difference in preparedness.
In addition to differences in attitude, our analysis also revealed a relationship between institutional policies and teacher confidence in using AI and teaching students to use AI. Teachers who had clear institutional policies around AI use also reported feeling more confident using AI for their own administrative tasks and in teaching students to use AI in a responsible way. At schools without clearly laid out policies, teachers reported less confidence in these areas.
A similar relationship also appeared for teachers reporting useful and relevant professional development opportunities centered around AI. Teachers who received useful AI professional development also reported feeling more comfortable using AI themselves and helping their students to use AI responsibly.
Notably, our results did not show a relationship between institutional policies or professional development and attitude towards teaching or concerns about academic dishonesty. It appears that the effect of institutional policy and professional development on these factors may be limited.
I spoke with teachers about AI. Here’s how the education system needs to adapt

Although it is perhaps not surprising that teachers who are trained on a new technology like AI feel more confident using it, it does serve as an important reminder that tailored professional development opportunities remain a vital tool in increasing teacher confidence around new technologies like AI.
In particular, the difference in attitude between disciplines makes the need for discipline-specific professional development opportunities clear. For English teachers, this may include professional development focused on designing assignments that cannot easily be written by AI and training students to use AI responsibly and ethically as part of the writing process. For math teachers, it might mean providing trainings centered on how AI can be used to free up time from administrative tasks like redesigning story problems or learning tasks.
Equally clear is the need for effective institutional level policies around both teacher and student AI use. Without clear institutional guidance on what type of AI use is permissible for teachers and students, teacher uncertainty around what is and is not acceptable AI use will continue.
The new grading system that’s dividing Washington teachers

It also remains important that institutional policies and professional development opportunities do not unthinkingly embrace AI technology without a consideration of how AI use might impact student learning. In their survey responses, many teachers expressed concern that student AI use might lead to cognitive declines in students, particularly when students are allowed to use AI in foundational courses that teach critical thinking.
Yet a considered approach remains necessary if we want teachers to make classroom-level decision rooted in student learning.
In roughly one-sixth of survey responses, teachers noted moving all writing to pen-and-paper, in-class writing assignments due to fears over academic dishonesty. Some teachers even wrote that they have stopped assigning homework entirely due to their belief that students are no longer completing assigned work without the use of AI.
Although these fears may reflect the feeling (reported by some teachers) that most of their students have stopped doing their work and are just using AI to complete assignments, these types of classroom decisions arguably take away opportunities for learning from the students who are doing their assigned work and trying to learn.
If math teachers had simply decided to stop teaching arithmetic because of the broad release of graphing calculators in the 1990s, student cheating may have gone down — but a whole generation of students would have also been left unprepared to do simple math.
From bell to bell, there is no cell! Teachers see benefits from classroom phone bans

Instead of reflexively rejecting or wholeheartedly embracing AI in the classroom, it is clear that a considered approach is essential. Clear institutional policies and high-quality discipline-specific training are both necessary to ensure we are making decisions rooted in student learning.We opened with the observation of one teacher who questioned whether teachers or students would remain relevant in the future. The findings of our study suggest that both remain indispensable.
AI may reshape teaching and learning in schools, but it does not eliminate the need for teacher judgment or student effort. Learning still depends on teachers making informed decisions about instruction and on students doing the intellectual work required to develop understanding.
Just as importantly, the best classrooms are built on relationships. Teachers encourage, challenge, and support students in ways that technology cannot.
As schools continue to navigate the opportunities and challenges presented by AI, the more important question may not be whether teachers and students remain relevant, but how AI can be used while preserving the human connections that inspire students to learn.
