name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s state budget wheels go round and round
description: Gov. Tate Reeves, left, discusses proposed revenue estimates with Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann during a meeting of the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, Wednesday, Nov. 15, 2023, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The process of developing a state budget for Mississippi is never-ending. There are steps in the process occuring nearly year-round.
Work in earnest – at least the work seen by the public – began last week on Mississippi’s $32-plus billion state budget to fund education, public healthcare, law enforcement, transportation and other services.
The 14-member Joint Legislative Budget Committee met publicly for two days to hear from some state agency leaders on their budget requests for the next fiscal year, which begins July 1.
Before the 2027 legislative session begins on Jan. 5 (always the first Tuesday after the first Monday of the year), the Budget Committee will develop a budget recommendation. That proposal serves as a guide or starting point for legislators when they meet in the new year to develop a plan to fund all state services.
Used to, the Budget Committee, which includes the lieutenant governor and speaker who alternate yearly as the chair of the panel, would meet for a month in late summer or early fall to hear from scores of state agencies about budget requests.
Now, the Budget Committee meets with a select few and depends on written requests that agency leaders had been working on during the summer. It is of note that the work on the next fiscal year’s budget begins behind the scenes for the agency leaders not long after the current budget year started on July 1.
In short, work on state agency budgets is a never-ending process.
One of the key steps in that process is when the Budget Committee and governor meet in the fall to develop a revenue estimate. That estimate represents the amount of revenue anticipated to be collected by the state during the upcoming fiscal year which runs  from July 1 until June 30 of the following year.
If actual revenue collections do not meet that estimate, the governor is forced to make mid-year budget cuts or dip into reserve funds to offset the shortfall.
During the legislative session, which begins in January, as stated earlier, the Legislature will work to appropriate the anticipated revenue to fund state services. The revenue estimate made by the governor and Budget Committee is important since knowing how much money is available is a crucial step in any budgeting process. But its importance is mitigated by the fact that the Budget Committee can, and often does, meet during the legislative session sans the governor to change that estimate.
At any rate, near the end of the three-month session (about four months the first year of every four-year term), legislators are supposed to come up with a budget.
Often, they have to extend the session or go into special session when they have disagreements or roadblocks to completing the budget, but it always gets done.
This current fiscal year, the overall state budget is a whopping $32.02 billion, including $13.11 billion in federal funds,
Federal funds make up a significant portion of the budgets for multiple state agencies, including Medicaid, Human Services, Environmental Quality and Transportation.
The portion of the budget that receives the most attention is the general fund (mostly revenue from such items as the sales tax, income tax and a litany of other taxes, including the so-called sin taxes on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling.) The general fund is often combined with the state-support funds, which include other taxes and revenue, such as  the 1-cent sales tax for education, the annual tobacco lawsuit settlement payments and others.
The general fund and state support funds total $9.22 billion. These are the funds legislators have the most discretion in how they are spent and are the funds that generally result in the most disagreements in the process.
The budget also is made up of $9.68 billion in special funds, generally fees or taxes to fund specific agencies. A lot of these agencies are small, such as boards that regulate various professions. The groups being regulated pay a fee to operate the agency. The largest special fund agency is the Department of Transportation, which is funded with a motor fuel tax and with federal funds.
There are multiple steps and moving parts associated with building a state budget each year. Yet, somehow those agencies are always funded.
And the budget cycle never stops.

name: VTDigger
title: An Essex County officials’ parking fight puts taxpayers in a tight spot
description:
Essex County’s sheriff and assistant judges are negotiating over justice center construction that could cost taxpayers more — whether work stops or continues.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  An Essex County officials’ parking fight puts taxpayers in a tight spot.
text:
The Essex County Courthouse in Guildhall, center, sits between the Meeting House (left) and the Essex County Sheriff’s Department on Wednesday, September 30, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Essex County’s sheriff and assistant judges have taken a simmering parking fight to court, leaving taxpayers caught between the cost of stopping construction and the risk of paying to redo it.
“Would it cost more to delay the project and design it correctly,” said Brice Simon, the sheriff’s attorney, “or would it cost more to do the project, find out later it wasn’t done quite right, and then have to deconstruct things and redo it?”
The dispute concerns changes to renovation plans for the Eben Judd Justice Center in Guildhall, a project that is projected to cost $4 million. The amended plan was approved by the Town Of Guildhall Planning Board on Aug. 27. Sheriff Trevor Colby argued that the revised plans for the parking area violate zoning laws and would hinder his department’s operations. 
Meanwhile, Evan Hammond and Kenn Stransky, two of the county’s assistant judges who lobbied for state approval and funding for the construction project, said that Colby lacks sufficient legal grounds for an appeal, while the project manager warns that delaying construction would drive up costs.
The outcome could determine both how the sheriff’s department operates at the renovated center and how much taxpayers ultimately pay for the work.
Colby filed his appeal of the permit on Sept. 4 with the Vermont Supreme Court Environmental Division, which handles local zoning disputes. At the initial Sept. 21 hearing, Judge Joseph McLean asked the parties to try to resolve the dispute through discussions before proceeding in court.
“It’s important for these different components of county government to be talking to each other and working with each other for any number of reasons, but not the least of which is the public perception,” McLean said in the Sept. 21 hearing.
Simon said he understood the judge’s concerns, but also saw a benefit in creating space for civil disagreements.
“On the one hand, ” Simon said, “it shows a healthy dialog between different branches of government that’s being conducted in a manner that, although has certain procedural formalities, it affords each side due process and a chance to be heard.”
Nicholas Low and Sarah Buxton are the attorneys representing the judges in the case, Hammond and Stransky. Low declined to comment on the record when asked about public perception of disputes between components of county government.
Colby argued in the initial appeal that the amended zoning permit for the renovation project violated the Guildhall Zoning Bylaw. The amended plan would affect a parcel of land not identified in the application or public notifications, Colby wrote.
The sheriff’s department is adjacent to that parcel of land, Colby wrote, and the changes would significantly impact the department’s ability to safely transport defendants into the building by reducing their parking capacity. 
Along with the reduced parking, the revised plan includes a retaining wall, which blocks the sheriff’s department’s access to the building from the private parking lot, Colby said in an interview. Deputies instead must walk around the wall and up a flight of stairs to access the office, he said.
“The further you have to walk somebody who’s intoxicated in handcuffs, or anybody we’re bringing in for processing … the more public safety risk is increased,” Colby said.
Colby is appealing on behalf of the sheriff’s department, Simon said in the initial hearing on Sept. 21.
Colby also asked to expedite the case and sought an immediate pause in construction on the parking element of the project to prevent work from being completed that might later need to be undone. 
McLean, the judge in the case, denied the stay request on Sept. 11 but agreed to expedite the case overall. To meet the requirements for a stay, the person must prove that “immediate and irreparable” harm will happen to them before the other side can be heard, according to his written statement. 
Colby’s appeal did not meet those standards, McLean wrote.
Stransky and Hammond, the county judges, lobbied for two years to get the project approved and funded by the state. Low filed a motion to dismiss the appeal Sept. 18.
The original plan would have expanded the sheriff’s department’s parking lot from 11 current spaces to 22, Colby said. But revisions made because of a design error raised the parking lot’s elevation, reduced the number of spaces and added a retaining wall, he said. The wall was installed before the appeal, Colby said.
The redesign was necessary for safety reasons because designers found a steeper elevation drop than originally anticipated between building the entrance and the parking area, Buxton said at a July 17 town board meeting, according to past reporting from the Caledonian Record. 
The revised plan changed the number of parking spots from 22 spots to nine, according to Colby’s motion for immediate stay and expedited consideration.
In his appeal, Colby claimed that he qualified for “interested-person status” under Vermont state law, because he continuously occupies the property adjoined to the construction site.
However, Low argued in his motion to dismiss that Colby did not have sufficient standing because the Vermont state law cited by Colby requires a “legal title or right to a property in the immediate neighborhood.”
“Reconfigured parking, altered pedestrian routes, and access changes to this public building will affect all members of the public equally,” Low wrote.
Project manager Zoltan Horvath wrote in a court document that a delay would increase costs because materials might need to be stored, the construction manager would need to be paid for extended time, and winter tends to add costs to construction projects. 
The dispute requires balancing those expenses against the potential cost of undoing construction of the parking area if Colby’s appeal succeeds, Simon said.
“If while you’re disputing that the person goes ahead and builds what they got a permit for, the horse’s left the barn,” Simon said. “And so the whole idea of a stay is to try to get the permit holder to have to stop the work so that you can then have your due process.”
Before the appeal can proceed further, Colby must establish standing, or show that he is sufficiently affected to bring the appeal, Low said.
“We think it’s enough of a question that, obviously, we brought it to the court,” Low said.
The court has not yet scheduled a date for the next hearing. Construction continues in the meantime, Colby said.
Low and Simon said they hope negotiations will resolve the dispute.
“Odds are we should be able to work something out,” Simon said. “If we can’t, the courts are there to make final decisions.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraskans describe frustration with state handling of childcare subsidy
description: OMAHA — Josh Wigginton and his wife each went to work Friday. One dropped off daughter Nayeli at their childcare center, which transports the 7-year-old to school and back. The other parent picked her up after the work day.  It’s a longtime routine that nearly collapsed earlier in the week due to what Wigginton said […]
text:
Nebraskans cite frustration with time and communication barriers in seeking approval of a public childcare subsidy in Nebraska as the state says they focus on fraud prevention and protecting taxpayer dollars. (Photo by Sue Barr/Getty Images)OMAHA — Josh Wigginton and his wife each went to work Friday. One dropped off daughter Nayeli at their childcare center, which transports the 7-year-old to school and back. The other parent picked her up after the work day. 
It’s a longtime routine that nearly collapsed earlier in the week due to what Wigginton said was an unusually long delay by the state to reauthorize the family’s annual childcare subsidy. 
“We’ve never had this problem before,” Wigginton said Tuesday, the day before they had to pay out of pocket or lose their spot at a Millard area childcare center. “An email to our caseworker came back undeliverable. I’ve been calling. I get hung up on. … I’m nervous.”
Josh and wife Amanda Wigginton with their children. (Courtesy of the Wiggintons)
The parents said they started the reauthorization process more than two months ago and were perplexed at the wait and complications because a subsidy was built in as part of their arrangement years ago when they adopted their then-foster child Nayeli. He said the couple eventually sent a second submission as a backup, and at one point his wife went in person to a state office and was told she needed to see someone else.
After the Nebraska Examiner inquired to the state Department of Health and Human Services Tuesday, the Wiggintons hours later got a call that their situation was resolved. That spared them from alternatives, which included a parent taking time off their job or calling on a grandparent to help.
But Nebraska advocates and service providers said other families statewide also have faced increased delays and communication barriers when seeking approval or reapproval for a childcare subsidy. It comes at a time when businesses, government leaders and policymakers are shining more light on rising childcare costs and inadequate access to quality and affordable services that help keep parents in the workforce.
“All of a sudden everything just kind of got backlogged,” said Shannon Burks, who owns Creative Corner Child Care in Grand Island. “I have some very frustrated parents.”
 ‘Big, beautiful’ 

The DHHS website states that approval of a subsidy for eligible families “may take up to six weeks to complete.” The full cost may be covered. Depending on income, some may owe a monthly fee paid directly to a qualified provider. The provider bills DHHS for the remainder. 
A DHHS spokesman acknowledged a “temporary” increase in processing times for programs including childcare subsidy approvals — and said it stems partly from stepped up eligibility restrictions called for in President Donald Trump’s “Big, Beautiful Bill,” which Congress approved in July 2025. 




Quotation







The move away from the honor system to verification for certain eligibility criteria is requiring more staff time to process.


– Jeff Powell, spokesperson for Nebraska Department of Social Services



Spokesman Jeff Powell said some resources that previously went to childcare subsidy applications have shifted to satisfy more stringent verification processes in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. SNAP now mandates all states to keep their error rate below 6% (Nebraska’s is at 5.9%) or face paying a greater share of the public benefits. 
Powell noted a focus on preventing fraud, protecting taxpayer dollars and ensuring benefits go to those who “truly need them.” 
“The move away from the honor system to verification for certain eligibility criteria is requiring more staff time to process,” he said.
Powell said DHHS, however, is “aggressively recruiting and hiring additional staff, which will soon alleviate workloads and improve processing times.” He said the agency has that green light, despite a hiring freeze that Gov. Jim Pillen requested of agencies to address a state budget deficit, 
Addressing the Wigginton case specifically, Powell said his team was reviewing the circumstances “and identifying any opportunities to improve communication and response times.” He said privacy requirements prohibit the state from discussing specifics, but a DHHS representative reached out to the family directly on Tuesday after the Examiner’s query.
Wigginton said he learned at that time that the family’s caseworker was no longer employed with the state, and that he has a new liaison.
“It’s a big pressure off of me,” he said afterward. He works in Fremont in a human relations role. His wife, Amanda, is a teacher. They have other kids and the childcare subsidy helps the family’s financial equation. “I feel bad for people who don’t know the process.”
Advocates at First Five Nebraska, which focuses on improving early childhood care through policy, said the most prevalent frustrations they’ve heard from service providers in the past several weeks are application processing times of 45 days to two months, sometimes longer, and phone calls with state representatives that have taken a couple of hours.
The First Five advocates said they recognize the complexities in verifying employment and other details. They cited one central Nebraska daycare facility and another in Omaha that each had about a third of their families awaiting subsidy approval at a given time. 
 ‘Hold my breath’ 

Tasha McNeil, director of Brilliant Brains Learning Center in Omaha, said she recently stepped in to help one of her daycare workers deal with her own family’s subsidy and was on the phone call for three hours and 41 minutes providing and verifying information to the state representative. The worker ultimately was reauthorized, but had to submit even more documentation. 
Kids play in a Omaha-based Kids Can center that expanded and opened in 2023. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
“They’re probably short-staffed,” McNeil said of the state. “But a lot of us are. That doesn’t stop us from having to do what we have to do.”
Burks, the Grand Island childcare operator, said she’s noticed more of  “a mess” and longer processing times in the last six months, which she said can put providers in a bind. 
Quick turnarounds are important to struggling families, advocates and providers said, noting that a lengthy wait for a subsidy approval could mean the difference between a parent taking a job or not.
Burks noted one father whose subsidy was up for renewal. She said he had just started a new job.
“He has two full-time kids here,” Burks said. “He has to pay (out of his own pocket) or I have to hold my breath and hope he gets covered.”
Justin Shapland, manager at the Wiggintons’ childcare center, said he appreciates the family but had to ask for private pay if the state didn’t approve the subsidy renewal by a certain date.
“I feel like everything is getting slow,” he said of state processing, including background checks for new hires. “I’d love to know what to do to make this go faster.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Democrats target Macomb County with a first-ever joint town hall featuring El-Sayed, Slotkin
description: The importance of Macomb County to Michigan Democrats’ 2026 playbook was on full display Saturday as U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin joined U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed for a joint town hall event that focused on unity, bridging the divide between moderates and progressives, and the outsized impact county residents could have on the election. As […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed (left) gives a fist bump to U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) during a town hall event on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026, in Warren, Mich. (Screenshot courtesy of C-SPAN)The importance of Macomb County to Michigan Democrats’ 2026 playbook was on full display Saturday as U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin joined U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed for a joint town hall event that focused on unity, bridging the divide between moderates and progressives, and the outsized impact county residents could have on the election.
As part of El-Sayed’s “Shouldn’t Be This Hard” town hall tour, the Democratic nominee heaped praise on Slotkin (D-Holly), noting that while they may not agree on some things, they do agree on the key hallmarks of Democratic Party values. They also share the belief, he said, that President Donald Trump’s tenure in the White House needs more forceful checks and balances from Democrats in Congress.
El-Sayed faces a tough battle against Republican U.S. Senate nominee and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake on Nov. 3. Slotkin previously defeated Rogers for the same office in 2024. No matter who wins, Slotkin will ascend to the role of the state’s senior senator.
Slotkin said Saturday that she needs El-Sayed in the role of junior senator if the Democrats plan to properly combat the abuses of the Trump administration and make real change for working families across Michigan.
“We have this fight over moderate versus progressive, or young versus old. And I want to tell you, being your senator for over 18 months, sitting in those rooms, that debate of moderate versus progressive is not the real debate,” Slotkin said. “The real debate among Democrats right now is fight versus flight. It is: Do you believe that in order to have the country we believe in, we got to fight for it? Or do you believe that if you just wait, Elissa — and I’ve had someone tell me this, ‘Elissa, politics is a long game. It’s cyclical. If you just wait, we don’t have any good tools right now. If you just wait, people will come back to us, and it’ll all be okay.’”
Slotkin said that simply wasn’t good enough, and that waiting out the Trump administration without any real pushback was not only a losing strategy for the party, it defies the wishes of the electorate that is looking for a real opposition party to the Republicans under Trump.
“I am on Team Fight,” Slotkin said. “And I need someone with me who is on Team Fight.”
Slotkin said that person was El-Sayed.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Democratic nominee opened his portion of the town hall with his usual campaign fare — dishing on the need for Medicare for All, the ravages of the Iran war on the American economy, and the urgency for the party to take back the U.S. Senate majority, not only to hold Trump accountable, but to also push back against his administration’s department heads.
El-Sayed has, in particular, expressed opposition to the policies of U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
On Slotkin, El-Sayed said the senator was “someone who does not back down, who does not hesitate to show up when people are in need, somebody who understands what it means to throw down when Michiganders need you to throw down.”
Slotkin, in a plea to voters, said that if El-Sayed wins, Michigan’s delegation would be the youngest in U.S. history, and they would also be the only delegation to have collectively rejected corporate PAC money in their respective campaigns for the U.S. Senate.
There’s also the possibility, should El-Sayed be victorious in November, that the delegation would be one that defeated the same Republican candidate for the same office in two back-to-back election cycles.
Slotkin said that would be an exciting proposition for voters, especially those in Macomb County. She added that she would not be a current U.S. senator without Macomb voters.
“You all have been the county, honestly, that decides more elections in the state of Michigan, and sometimes more elections than the entire country,” Slotkin said. “People know the name Macomb County, like even when they don’t live in the state of Michigan. You all are the deciders in many of our elections, and I only won because we did a couple of clicks better here.”
El-Sayed said that Macomb County typically gets put in the “red” category, but he’s betting on changing the narrative.
“I don’t see any ‘red’ folks here. Frankly, I don’t see any ‘blue’ folk here either,” El-Sayed said. “I see folks who are sick and tired of watching the president make light of our plights. I see folks who are sick and tired of having to worry about how they’re going to afford next month’s rent. … I see folks who are ready to get out the vote every day for the next 30 days.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Republicans can’t stop talking about banning trans athletes
description: This story was originally reported by Brooke Migdon of The 19th. Meet Brooke and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. Speaking to a crowd of supporters in central Florida in August, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds denounced his soon-to-be general election opponent for governor, Democrat David Jolly, as a “Trojan horse” for […]
text:
A protester raises a fist beside a large transgender pride flag at the Kentucky State Capitol. (Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)
This story was originally reported by Brooke Migdon of The 19th.  Meet Brooke and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
Speaking to a crowd of supporters in central Florida in August, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds denounced his soon-to-be general election opponent for governor, Democrat David Jolly, as a “Trojan horse” for progressive politics in the reliably red state.
“David Jolly is somebody who thinks it’s still OK for boys to be in girls’ sports,” said Donalds, purposefully misgendering transgender girls. “Just pure insanity.” A day later, he secured the Republican nomination.
In a Facebook post earlier that week, the Republican Party of Florida had claimed “boys WILL be allowed to compete in girls’ sports” if Jolly, a former Republican congressman who has objected to sweeping state bans on trans student-athletes, is elected in November. The group shared a video of an AI-generated brawny, masculine figure in a women’s bathing suit smirking on a winner’s podium, strutting through a women’s locker room and ripping open a shower curtain.
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL) talks with fellow Republicans on Jan. 3, 2023, after the new Congress failed to elect a new Speaker of the House Donalds was nominate for Speaker the next day in a largely symbolic gesture. Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) was elected Speaker after 15 votes. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
“Will I have to race someone like that one day?” a young girl asks in the video. “David Jolly says we have to let them play,” her mother replies.
But Jolly, who secured the Democratic nomination for governor last month, would not have the authority to do so: Florida law has prohibited trans student-athletes from joining sports teams that match their gender identity for more than five years. Jolly has said he has “no plans” to change the current law.
In Georgia’s competitive governor’s race, Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson has launched nearly identical attacks against his Democratic opponent, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta.
“Keisha Lance Bottoms thinks boys should play girls’ sports. That’s just crazy,” Jackson wrote on his campaign’s official Facebook page in April. He reiterated his criticism of Bottoms in another social media post in June, writing that his opponent “has no problem with boys playing girls’ sports,” and denouncing her position that athletic governing bodies, rather than politicians, should set eligibility requirements.
But Georgia, too, has long banned trans students from teams matching their gender identity.
The Georgia High School Association, which oversees high school sports in the state, voted unanimously in 2022 to designate sports teams based on students’ sex assigned at birth, and legislation signed by Republican Gov. Brian Kemp last spring prohibits trans athletes from competing on teams that match their gender identity from kindergarten through college. (Nationally, the NCAA has barred trans women from competing in women’s collegiate sports since February 2025).
Rebekah Bruesehoff, a transgender student athlete, speaks at a press conference on LGBTQI+ rights, at the U.S. Capitol on March 8, 2023. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
In governors races across the country, Republican candidates have rallied against inclusive sports policies — even in states where limitations on trans athletes have been in place for years.
Claims that Democrats support allowing trans athletes to compete flew during a recent gubernatorial debate in Kansas, where trans girls have been barred from competing in girls’ and women’s sports since 2023. Candidates’ positions on trans athletes have even emerged as a talking point in the race for Indiana secretary of state — a position with no lawmaking ability in a state where trans students have been prohibited from competing in line with their gender identity since 2022.
In June, after narrowly clinching the Republican nomination for governor of Iowa, private school founder Zach Lahn claimed Democrat Rob Sand would be “willing” to allow trans student-athletes to join teams matching their gender identity, despite a state law that has prohibited them from doing so since 2022.
Some Democrats have recently voiced support for restrictions on trans athletes, but “it’s Republicans that are bringing it up,” said Lanae Erickson, senior vice president at Third Way, a centrist Democratic advocacy group and think tank. “Republicans don’t have much else to run on. They’re not going to run on the economy, and the dynamics on immigration, politically, have shifted. So, this is kind of their last bet, and they are playing it literally everywhere.”
Sand, Iowa’s state auditor since 2019, has said in interviews that he does not support allowing trans students to compete in line with their gender identity. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton drew outrage and disappointment from LGBTQ+ groups over the summer when she told a local newspaper that she would “not support boys playing in girls’ sports” as governor, citing a 2024 state law that already bars trans women and girls from K-12 and collegiate sports.
The landscape for transgender students in sports has shifted dramatically in just a short time: Idaho, the first to enact explicit statewide restrictions on trans athletes, did so only in 2021. More than half the nation has since adopted similar restrictions, and President Donald Trump has made barring trans women and girls from female sports nationally a central policy focus of his second administration.
Arkansas governor signs executive order prioritizing state law over new Title IX rule

State and federal lawsuits against both restrictive and inclusive policies have yielded mixed results. In June, the Supreme Court ruled that states can lawfully bar trans student-athletes from competing in line with their gender identity.
But voters in states with restrictive laws may not be entirely aware of those policies, experts said, and candidates are cashing in on the confusion.
“People feel that the status quo is very chaotic, and they don’t know what their state’s rules are,” said Erikson. “They see media coverage of an instance of a transgender person competing somewhere in America, and they don’t really think about whether that is in Ohio or in Iowa.”
Campaigns have very little incentive to correct the record, said Andrew Flores, an associate professor of government at American University. “They’re trying to be persuasive,” he said. “They’re not trying to be fact-oriented.”
Other voters may know their state’s policies but prioritize national politics.
“Given our media environment, people are thinking far less about what’s going on locally than what’s going on nationally,” Flores said. “As long as people are convinced that this is still a national issue, as opposed to a local issue, then campaigns can still try and run on the issue even if, technically, it’s a non-issue in their district or state.”
Nationally, Republican-aligned groups are betting big on anti-trans messaging ahead of November’s midterms, seeking to capitalize on public opinion polls that show most Americans favor separating sports teams by sex assigned at birth.
More than three dozen ads released since the beginning of September by America PAC, the super PAC created and funded by Elon Musk, for instance, hammer Democrats over the party’s once-broad support for trans rights, including when it comes to sports. Musk, the world’s richest person, plans to spend at least $100 million to help elect Republicans this fall, the New York Times reported in July.
“Republican politicians are banking on the fact that the majority of Americans may not know that they know a trans person, or may not know anything about what it means to be trans,” said Zein Murib, an associate professor of political science at Fordham University. “They have an opportunity to set the agenda, or at the very least exploit that lack of knowledge about trans people.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Debates used to mean something in Arkansas politics. Now they’re an afterthought.
description: Seeking a breakout moment in his bid to unseat Mark Pryor in Arkansas’ nationally watched Senate race 12 years ago, Tom Cotton borrowed an idea from the 19th century. Cotton challenged the two-term Democratic incumbent to a series of debates patterned after the 1858 meetings between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas. With no moderators or […]
text:
The Arkansas PBS debate between candidates for the United States Senate was held on Oct. 21, 2022 at the Donald W. Reynolds Performance Hall, on the University of Central Arkansas campus in Conway. The participants, from left, are: Libertarian candidate Kenneth Cates, Democratic candidate Natalie James, and Republican incumbent John Boozman. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Seeking a breakout moment in his bid to unseat Mark Pryor in Arkansas’ nationally watched Senate race 12 years ago, Tom Cotton borrowed an idea from the 19th century.
Cotton challenged the two-term Democratic incumbent to a series of debates patterned after the 1858 meetings between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas. With no moderators or panelists, the two candidates would instead ask each other questions.
“There used to be a time in our politics when voters could look the two candidates in the eye and hear from them directly — that’s what I’m inviting Sen. Pryor to participate in today,” Cotton said.
The Lincoln-Douglas-style debates never materialized, and the two instead squared off in other televised formats with moderators and panelists before Cotton won the race that fall.
Now that he’s seeking reelection, Cotton is a lot less nostalgic for old-fashioned faceoffs. The two-term Republican has declined debates with Democratic rival Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin on public television and on Arkansas State University’s campus, opting instead for one hosted by a conservative Christian media outlet.
That comes in a midterm environment where President Trump’s low approval numbers have given some Democrats hope they can pull off an upset in a solidly red state. 
Cotton’s decision isn’t a surprising one, and is a symptom of a larger problem in Arkansas politics. Once considered a rite of passage for candidates, Arkansas debates were among the few unscripted moments of drama on the campaign trail.
Now, they’ve become an afterthought. 



Let us know what you think...


 


Arkansas history is filled with examples of debate moments that shook up a race or helped candidates get more traction. One of the most famous was the 1972 debate between Sen. John McClellan and then-U.S. Rep. David Pryor, Mark Pryor’s late father. 
After forcing McClellan into a runoff for the Democratic nomination, David Pryor challenged the incumbent lawmaker to a debate. McClellan used the faceoff to challenge Pryor’s ties to organized labor and went on to win the nomination.
Pryor, who was elected to the Senate in 1978, said the loss and debate performance stung years later.
“I appeared naive and inexperienced, he appeared the seasoned veteran,” Pryor wrote in his autobiography.
Debates have offered Arkansas voters an early look at politicians, even if they don’t win the election. Asa Hutchinson’s surprisingly strong debate performance against then-Sen. Dale Bumpers in 1986 didn’t win him the race, but it earned the attention of political observers impressed with how he fared against a political giant.
Years later, Hutchinson and Mike Beebe repeatedly laid out their differences in a series of debates and forums in the months leading up to the 2006 gubernatorial election. Beebe won that race, and Hutchinson succeeded his former rival eight years later.
Those appearances didn’t necessarily decide the 2006 governor’s race. Neither did Cotton’s debates with Mark Pryor, though the incumbent lawmaker’s answer to a question about how he’d define the middle class offered Cotton additional lines of attack in the race.
But those appearances gave voters a chance to see the clear policy differences in both races. Beebe and Hutchinson split in those debates on how they’d approach education, tax cuts and other issues. The Cotton-Pryor meetings underscored the heated nature of the race and showed the dividing line on healthcare. 
With questions about the economy, the war in Iran, fuel prices and many other issues looming, voters deserve as many chances as possible to see the Senate candidates debate.
That’s also true in the governor’s race, where Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has agreed to only one debate with Democrat Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby on Arkansas TV. Sanders did not appear with the two during the Arkansas Press Association’s debate over the summer.
When candidates limit the number of debates they participate in — or outright refuse to debate — voters miss out on seeing the differences between candidates and how they respond to tough questions about their stances. It’s the kind of interaction that can’t be captured in a 30-second ad or dueling social media messages written by campaign staff.
The types of debates Lincoln and Douglas engaged in, complete with hourlong opening statements that drew thousands of spectators in person, may be a relic from another political time. 
If candidates aren’t willing to face each other and answer questions, debates themselves could face the same fate in Arkansas.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Casselton-area residents question data center location on prime farmland
description: CASSELTON, N.D. — Caryn Weber said she is not against data centers, but questions the location of a proposed site in rural Cass County.  “It’s disturbing to see prime farmland covered up with concrete,” Weber said Thursday inside Bondegard Cafe in downtown Casselton.  Representatives of Geronimo Power, the company behind a proposed data center east […]
text:
Vince Sakraida, director of data center engineering for Geronimo Power, speaks with a visitor at the Bondegard Cafe in Casselton, North Dakota, on Oct. 1, 2026. The company was sharing information about its planned data center. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)CASSELTON, N.D. — Caryn Weber said she is not against data centers, but questions the location of a proposed site in rural Cass County. 
“It’s disturbing to see prime farmland covered up with concrete,” Weber said Thursday inside Bondegard Cafe in downtown Casselton. 
Representatives of Geronimo Power, the company behind a proposed data center east of Casselton and north of Mapleton, answered questions about the Harmony Energy Park project at the cafe. 
2nd Fargo-area data center would use double the power of Harwood site

Data centers have become a main topic of discussion in North Dakota with more events on deck in Cass County. 
Tuesday, the Legislature’s Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meets at 9 a.m. at Grand Farm, near Casselton. The agenda includes water use by data centers, data center impact on local government and testimony from utility officials.
The following week, on Oct. 14, North Dakota State University is hosting a data center discussion in Fargo. “Powering the AI Economy: Data Centers and North Dakota’s Future” will be hosted by NDSU’s Challey Institute for Global Innovation and Growth. The event is in the NDSU Memorial Union starting at 5:30 p.m.
Panelists include North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring and Paul Matthys, president and CEO of Cass County Electric Cooperative.
Goehring, a Republican, is being challenged by Democrat Vern Thompson, who has made data centers a top issue in the ag commissioner race. 
North Dakota residents have expressed concerns about noise, water use, utility rates and the loss of farmland.
Handouts from Geronimo Power about its proposed data center lie on a table in the Bondegard Cafe in Casselton, North Dakota, on Oct. 1, 2026. The company was meeting with local residents about its plans. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
In Casselton on Thursday, Geronimo representatives handed out information to address those questions and why the company wants to put a data center in Harmony Township.
The company cites the area as being at a crossroads of electric and gas infrastructure. The data center would need as much as 540 megawatts of power at peak demand.
That infrastructure would include the Bison Substation, a solar farm Geronimo is building next to the substation, a planned battery storage site to go with the solar farm and a natural gas pipeline coming from western North Dakota. MDU Resources announced last week that it would go ahead with the Bakken East Pipeline, though an exact route has not been finalized. 
Samantha Burchill, an NDSU student whose parents live near the proposed data center site, said she is not opposed to data centers, but said the rural countryside doesn’t make sense. 
She said she recently toured the Applied Digital data center under construction near Harwood north of Fargo and found it “very depressing.” 
Burchill’s father, Dustin Burchill, became chair of the Harmony Township Board of Supervisors in September, as details about the data center plan emerged. Her mother, Sarah Burchill, spoke out at a community meeting in Casselton, advocating for “family farms before data farms.”   
Samantha Burchill, left, and Marjie Broden, wait to order food at the Bondegard Cafe in Casselton, North Dakota, on Oct. 1, 2026. Representatives of Geronimo Energy were sharing information about the company’s planned data center. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Samantha Burchill was at the cafe with Marjie Broden, who farms land in Harmony Township near the proposed site, though she lives in a neighboring township.
Broden said she wished she had known about plans for the project much earlier. 
“We need a lot more time to decide something like this,” she said. 
Geronimo filed its application for a conditional use permit in Harmony Township on Sept. 15. 
 


Broden said she is in support of a temporary moratorium on data centers that was discussed by the Harmony Township Board of Supervisors on Sept. 22.
“There is a place for data centers, but it sure as heck is not in the heart of the Red River Valley, some of the nicest cropland in the United States,” she said.
The township board will meet next on Oct. 20.
The North Dakota Public Service Commission has no authority over data center siting, but it will need to approve the battery storage site. It is holding a public hearing in Casselton on Oct. 23.
A Geronimo representative said more than 200 people came to the cafe Thursday. 
“Our vision is to develop this project thoughtfully, addressing local priorities while creating lasting benefits including new jobs, expanded tax revenue and growth for local businesses,” the company said in a statement. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Where exactly is Canaan, Conn.? There are at least two answers
description: North Canaan and Canaan, towns stacked just below the Massachusetts border, are used to being mixed up. But the names create real problems.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

A man walks into Canaan’s town hall to meet with his probation officer — but the probation officer isn’t there.
He didn’t get the time or date wrong, he got the actual town wrong. The man was supposed to meet his probation officer in North Canaan’s town hall, which is, fittingly, just a few miles north.
Johanna Mann, Canaan’s town clerk, wasn’t surprised by the mix-up. Official records meant for North Canaan come across her desk all the time.
“I think at this point, a [name change] would solve the confusion,” Mann said. “But I understand the history.” 

Town of Canaan Selectman Judy Jacobs laughs as she answers a question at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

North Canaan and Canaan, two Connecticut towns stacked just below the Massachusetts border, are used to being mixed up. That’s because Canaan is locally known as “Falls Village,” and North Canaan, in classic nickname style, prefers a simple “Canaan.” These unofficially official names are used everywhere short of some maps — even some state road signage refers to the towns by their nicknames.
While it may seem trivial, these town names create real problems. Land records, birth records, death records — even the amount of revenue sent to towns from the state tax on nips, the small bottles of alcohol — are confused. And snail-mail is a whole other issue.
“They have Canaan on their post office, and here we’ve got Falls Village on the post office,” Judy Jacobs, a selectman for Canaan and president of the historical society for the two towns, said. “But the government still recognizes us as town of Canaan and them as town of North Canaan. So it’s really, really confusing.”

Town of Canaan Selectman Judy Jacobs Looks at a map of the town of Canaan from 1853 at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The source of the confusion
For more than 100 years, the two towns were one united Canaan. But in 1858, they broke up.
“Basically, it stemmed from the convenience of getting to church,” Jacobs said. “People had to travel quite a distance to go to church in both directions, so they ended up dividing.”
The original town of Canaan was settled in 1738. But talks of division, at least informally, began shortly after. There was a religious division — involving two Ecclesiastical Societies — in 1769. Initial proposals to break the sprawling 52.7-square-mile town into two were recorded in 1810.
It took the local government decades to finalize the divide, but when it finally did, one town received the name North Canaan and the other Canaan.
These names stuck for a while, Jacobs said. The church was moved south, to Canaan, and North Canaan residents built their own churches. And nobody had to take a five-mile trek to get to their church.
But the Housatonic Railroad created a stop in Canaan called Falls Village, after the Great Falls located in the town. And from then on, the two towns would be forever confused.
“So, it became Falls Village and North Canaan, and then North Canaan just shortened themselves to Canaan,” Jacobs said. “It got really confusing.”
In 1968, historian Nellie Rodgers attempted to document the history of the split, which has early roots in the history of the state. But even 58 years ago, Rodgers flagged the name debacle in her work.
“Except for the confusion with the names, things seem to be satisfactory,” Rodgers wrote in a July 1968 work titled “A History of The Division of The Town of Canaan.”
“The names, North Canaan and Canaan, confusing even to the State of Connecticut, may some day be resolved. What action will ensue, I cannot predict,” Rodgers continued. “But if change does occur, to eliminate the confusion now taking place, then another chapter will have to be added to the present town division history.”
But Rodgers never added another chapter. 

A sign saying “Entering Falls Village” at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Data collection, death certificates and signs
On the same day of the probation officer mix-up, Mann, attending to her official town clerk duties in Canaan — er, Falls Village — opened a land record. But it was for land located in North Canaan.
These very common mix-ups actually result in increased postage fees for Canaan, Mann said. Birth certificates, death certificates, marriage certificates and firearms paperwork for North Canaan come across her desk all the time.
Every time she receives a record meant for their neighboring town, Mann either sends these records back to the original sender, sends them to the correct town or requests help in correcting digital data.
“If you’re part of anything in the town government, you realize,” Jacobs said. “If you’re a business owner, you realize. If you get your mail messed up, you figure it out. And any newcomer using GPS … they get very confused.”
In order to get ahead of at least some of this confusion, Mann has changed her name tag three times. The first one just listed her town as Canaan, CT. The other two include some variation of the name Falls Village.

Johanna Mann is the Canaan town clerk. She remade her name tag three times, all with different variations of the town’s names.  Credit: Sasha Allen / CT Mirror

People who did not grow up in one of the two towns tend to have the most trouble, Jacobs said. 
“When you go to school here, it’s kind of pounded into your brain that you’re the town of Canaan, Falls Village,” Jacobs said. “When you’ve grown up here, you quickly figure it out. But it’s hard for newcomers. They’re just like, ‘What? Where am I?'”
It’s not just the town names — within North Canaan is a small village called Canaan. Among the two towns, there are numerous unofficial (and sometimes mostly forgotten) villages: Canaan Valley, East Canaan, South Canaan, Canaan and Falls Village are among the most confusing. And then there’s the village of Sodom, in North Canaan.
To make matters worse, the Canaan and North Canaan share some road names. “Main Street” and “Railroad Street” are fitting for both, but the two towns also have a “Prospect Street.”
Some of the state road signage, which seemingly welcomes folks into multiple towns at once, doesn’t help.
So, it’s no wonder newcomers, and their GPS systems, are easily confused.
Real-world implications
This confusion isn’t limited to just Connecticut newcomers. These nicknames trick state officials, too.
A recent mix-up resulted in some of North Canaan’s money being sent to Canaan from the nip tax. This tax, which charged an extra 5 cents on every nip sold in a liquor store, was supposed to be returned to the municipality where the product was purchased.
Canaan, which is home to just one liquor store, was selling an average of 136,612 nips per year and getting nearly $10,000 in annual revenue, according to state data.
But the town’s lone liquor store — Falls Village Package Store — was definitely not selling more than 136,000 nips each year. 
Instead, two other liquor stores, Stateline Wine and Spirits and Canaan Liquors, were incorrectly listed as Canaan establishments by the Wine and Spirits Wholesalers of Connecticut. These two stores are actually in the town of North Canaan but in the village of Canaan. Since they’re in Canaan village, the address of the two stores shows up on Google maps as Canaan, CT.
The state corrected its error and now is distributing the revenue correctly. But this is just one of many possible issues caused by the names.
“I understand that it causes problems,” Michelle Hansen, the Canaan town treasurer said. “Believe me, it does. Our fire department gets dispatched to calls that are actually in North Canaan, not on Main Street.”
Hansen is also the emergency management director for Canaan. She said that, especially when a dispatcher is unfamiliar with the two towns, emergency services can be sent to the wrong location.
But her department has found ways to combat the issue. 
“I have a list that I have at home at work to look it up and see if the address is really ours,” Hanson said. “We’ve found a way to combat it pretty quickly and pretty easily so it doesn’t cause a delay in services.”
Even Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program data is likely incorrect. In 2022, the state recorded that 211 Canaan residents, or 19.5% of the population, were enrolled in the program. But 37 North Canaan residents, or 1.18% of its population, were recorded as enrolled in the program.
North Canaan has nearly three times Canaan’s population and has a lower median household income than its southern neighbor — making it unlikely that Canaan has nearly six times more SNAP recipients.
A 2024 Canaan housing profile from the Partnership for Strong Communities recorded that there were 583 federally assisted housing units in Canaan. But Hansen said the town only has three apartment buildings. And with just over 1,000 residents living in the town, some Canaan residents believe the number is likely inflated.
Vaccination numbers during COVID were also inflated — with more than 1,300 Canaan residents recorded as vaccinated as of February 2023 in a town of just over 1,000 residents.
Even with these issues, the proposal to change the name of one or both of the towns is still up for debate.

Town of Canaan Selectman Judy Jacobs looks over items from World War I on display at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

To change or not to change
Hansen believes renaming Canaan as Falls Village could be even worse.
“I actually think changing it at this point would cause just as much of a nightmare as what it is,” Hanson said. “People know us as the town of Canaan, Falls Village, and if we were just to go to Falls Village, people are still going to call us the town of Canaan.”
Hansen also said the change would be a huge administrative lift. The town would have to change the names on letterheads, checks and stamps.
As for the emergency response side of things, changing the name could create an even bigger headache. 
“As emergency management director, all of my emergency plans and everything are for the town of Canaan,” Hansen said. “I can’t imagine changing all that to Falls Village.”
Jacobs said getting the name changed is difficult. Canaan would have to go through the state legislature to approve a name change, and all divisions of state and local government would have to make the administrative changes.
North Canaan has also discussed a name change. When the town of North Canaan put up signs that read “Welcome to Canaan,” Jacobs said they were encouraged to seek an official name change. Officially, though, the town is still named North Canaan.
As for the official town of Canaan — unofficial town of Falls Village — Hansen’s view is popular.
“A lot of people say, ‘Well, this is how we are historically. We are the town of Canaan,'” Jacobs said. 
But Jacobs herself takes a slightly different stance. 
“And I am a diehard historian for the town,” Jacobs said, “but I think we should be called Falls Village. If we could find someone to take this on, this challenge … I think most of the residents would agree with that.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The AI data center push has roiled Kansas politics. It may also define the race for governor.
description: Cindy Holscher has something she would like you to know. She changed her mind on data centers because she listens. “The subject was coming up over and over again,” she said of the 80 or so town halls she held in the last 12 months across Kansas. “It seemed to me at the time that […]
text:
Cindy Holscher, the Deomcratic nominee for Kansas governor, listens to teachers during a campaign stop on Sept. 27 in Emporia. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Cindy Holscher has something she would like you to know.
She changed her mind on data centers because she listens.
“The subject was coming up over and over again,” she said of the 80 or so town halls she held in the last 12 months across Kansas. “It seemed to me at the time that a lot of candidates were really wary of this subject and hadn’t figured out this was something people cared about.”
When Holscher, a state senator from Overland Park, won the primary to become the Democratic nominee for governor two months ago, it was partly fueled by her call for a state moratorium on new data center construction. Since then, public concern over data centers and alarm about artificial intelligence have accelerated, turning a wild card in the primary into what may be a defining issue for the governor’s race in Kansas and midterms across the country.
The data center divide is just one disagreement among many between Holscher and her opponent, Senate President Ty Masterson, an Andover Republican. But in a political climate where party lines have been scrambled because of populist resistance to big tech, it may prove a bigger factor than anyone would have guessed just a few months ago.
Masterson’s campaign acknowledged, but did not otherwise respond, to an emailed request from me for an in-person interview about data centers.
“You know, there’s a lot of great possibilities with A.I.,” Holscher told me during a Sept. 27 campaign stop at Emporia, “but when I talk to people like the teachers who were just here, it’s about the anxiety in terms of what it might mean for the future, what it might be in terms of job loss. And that’s something that’s not talked about much, because the focus has been on energy and water usage.”
Holscher had just spoken to a group of local educators about their concerns. She did more listening than talking, sometimes jotting notes, at other times offering a few words to acknowledge what the teachers were saying. Listening is not an easy skill, but Holscher looked at ease doing it.
She defeated Democratic rival Ethan Corson by 10 points in the August primary. Corson, a Johnson County attorney and political moderate, attempted to frame the contest in a PBS Kansas gubernatorial primary debate as a choice between someone who could hold the governorship for the Democrats in a deep red state and somebody who could not.
Corson was endorsed by outgoing governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat at the end of her second term. Kelly was propelled to office by voter distaste for the legacy of the failed economic tax-cutting “experiment” of former governor Sam Brownback, but she was often stymied during her tenure from expanding Medicaid and other issues by the Republican supermajorities in the Kansas Legislature. Kelly, a promoter of bipartisanship and big-ticket economic development, embraced some big-ticket initiatives, including coaxing the Kansas City Chiefs across the state line with a tax incentive package that included a billion dollars in public funding.
Holscher opposed the final deal to bring the Chiefs to Kansas.
It wasn’t the only time she and Kelly were at odds.
Holscher revealed some internecine fighting when she vented on social media that she and two other Democrats were told by the Kelly administration to stand aside for another candidate, a claim the governor’s chief of staff told the Kansas Reflector was a mischaracterization. Holscher said that such insider manipulation has frustrated many voters about Kansas Democrats.
After her primary win, the New York Times described Holscher as an “outspoken populist” who took on data centers and the political status quo. Some of the criticism leveled at Holscher by fellow Democrats during the primary campaign, that she was perhaps too far left, has been taken up and amplified by Masterson.
During the gubernatorial debate last month at the Kansas State Fair at Hutchinson, Masterson called her a socialist and the “most radical liberal progressive that’s ever been on a ticket.” Holscher responded by reminding Masterson to his support of the Brownback experiment, which defunded Kansas schools “to the crisis point.”
Masterson also challenged Holscher’s change of mind on data centers.
“My position has never changed,” Masterson said about data centers during the televised debate. “It’s about guardrails first.”
Masterson said guardrails were already in place thanks to S.B. 98, enacted in 2025. It shields consumers from electricity rate increases, he said, and protects the water and the land from pollution. He also urged decisions on data centers to be made at the local level.
“Let the locals decide,” he said. “There are places where they don’t make sense and places where they do make sense.” Why wouldn’t a city want significant property tax relief through data centers, he asked.
Holscher was an example of a “perfect politician” who flip-flips on an issue, he said, because she originally voted in favor of the measure encouraging data centers and now opposes them.
Masterson bowed out of two additional televised debates with Holscher, saying the public had already seen them together in multiple platforms. Both parties claimed victory in the state fair debate. So far, Masterson’s campaign has been largely conventional for a Kansas Republican, driven chiefly by a promise to stop “runaway” property taxes.
Masterson, who has the endorsement of Donald Trump, might have a difficult time changing his mind on data centers even if he wanted to. Allowing any daylight between himself and Trump, who has doubled down on data centers, could be taken by the president as a sign of disloyalty. And Trump’s enthusiastic messaging on data centers and artificial intelligence offers little room for nuance.
Communities that reject data centers, Trump said recently, will end up “backwards and poor.” But a Gallup poll from earlier this year indicates that about 70% of Americans don’t want AI data centers in their areas. More recent polling says 58% of voters believe new data center construction will have a negative effect on the country.
Trump has relied on tech oligarchs for money, influence, and the 2025 chainsaw attack on the federal government. A cheerleader for AI (which he would like to rebrand as “super intelligence”), Trump recently announced an “accord” in which tech giants agreed to police themselves on AI safety and development. But self-policing hasn’t worked for the Catholic Church, Wall Street, or the police. It didn’t work with nuclear weapons. We shouldn’t expect it to work for the players in the new AI smarts race, especially when humanity already seems to be lurching toward a silicon-spawned human extinction event.
That catastrophe seemed closer to hand Oct. 1 when the Trump Pentagon named Elon Musk, the wealthiest person in the world, the wielder of the DOGE chainsaw and the owner of xAI, to co-lead a 120-day project on the future of technology in warfare. This move is especially alarming, considering the U.S. and Russia recently colluded to block progress on a United Nations draft of an AI weapons pact, according to the Washington Post. Language that would have required human approval before AI pulled the trigger on enemies it had targeted were removed.
Presumably Masterson does not want to unleash autonomous killer bots on humanity, but he’s not urging caution, either. Aligning oneself with the Trump administration’s stance on AI leaves little room for a thoughtful consideration of the ethical and humanitarian concerns. As for Masterson’s call for allowing locals to decide whether to allow data centers in their communities? That sounds reasonable until you consider that some local governments in Kansas are vigorously pursuing data center projects, public opinion be damned.
In my town of Emporia, city officials have so far advanced a proposed data center at every step since it was announced June 2, despite fierce organized resistance. There were sign-waving protests, testimony at public hearings that ran about 8-1 against the project, and a flurry of petition drives. Two of those petitions were successful and resulted in Nov. 3 ballot measures that would, if they survive legal challenges, ban high-impact data centers and battery energy storage systems for 10 years. Other petitions seek a grand jury investigation and changing the city’s form of government.
Questions about data centers are also on the ballot in other Kansas communities, including Ottawa and El Dorado. Citizen-led groups elsewhere, including De Soto and Edgerton, are also seeking to place the issue before voters.
Resistance to data centers is a new phenomenon, and a year ago it wasn’t on the radar of pollsters and politicians in Kansas. A Democratic lawmaker from central Kansas told me in an informal conversation recently that when he voted for S.B. 98, he didn’t hear a peep of opposition from anybody.
Most state legislators voted for the measure, enacted in 2025, which provides a 20-year state and local tax exemption for data centers that meet certain criteria, including an investment of $250 million, a 10-year electrical utility partnership, and a promise to create 20 full-time jobs within two years of commencing operations.
During the final vote in the Kansas Senate on April 11, 2025, only one senator – Tory Marie Blew, a Barton County Republican – voted against it. In the Kansas House, the month before, 15 Democrats and two Republicans voted “nay.”
In the Fall 2025 “Kansas Speaks” statewide opinion survey, released a year ago this month, questions about artificial intelligence were limited to how people used the technology in their daily life and in their work. There were no questions about how state residents regarded the technology or whether they would support construction of a data center nearby.
In fact, the term “data center” does not appear in the survey.
Thirty-seven percent of respondents in the 2025 survey said they did not use AI at all. Another 18% were unsure if they did, and the remainder — about half of all respondents — said they used generative or non-generative AI in their daily lives.
The “Kansas Speaks” survey for Fall 2026 has not yet been released.
Holscher told me the gubernatorial race was a choice between a candidate who represented the people and one propped up by money from big tech companies. AI super PACs had spent more than $800,000 in support of  Masterson’s campaign, she said. When she mentioned the money she seemed a bit less at ease, perhaps because she’s being badly outspent.
She’s also trailing in the polls, according to the New York Times.
But the difference is single digits.
As Bob Beatty, a political science professor puts it, Holscher is an underdog who must do what no Democrat in 144 years of state history has done: replace a fellow Democrat as governor who is leaving office. Holscher, he said, is Rocky Balboa to Masterson’s Apollo Creed. As Beatty reminds us, Rocky didn’t win in the first movie.
Since 2016, I haven’t put much faith in polls, as we’ve been badly misled too many times. We’re also still a month out from the election, which is almost forever in political time.
Holscher told me the affordability crisis is still foremost among the issues for her campaign, but that the more she learns about artificial intelligence and data centers, the more concerned she becomes. She wasn’t optimistic about meaningful national regulation on AI, she said, considering the current administration.
She would reconsider her vote on S.B. 98 if she could.
“At the time, it was presented as a picture of all the potential economic development it would bring, what it would do for our communities,” she said. “But things look different, 15 or 16 months later, with new information and hearing from people across the state.”
Those who are pushing back against data centers and demanding more transparency from local governments are going the right thing, Holscher said, because the system is meant to turn on citizen engagement. She said she didn’t set a time limit for her moratorium, because she did not yet know how long would be enough to get some clarity. It might take six months, she said.
It might take longer.
The important thing, she said, was for the state to take the lead in establishing better safeguards for new data center construction so that communities could follow.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Your next car will be a luxury
description: The average price of a new car is now $50,089. That puts in it CT's 7.75% luxury tax category.
text:
It’s been a busy week on the transportation beat. Not much of it good:
Cheaper cars? The U.S. Dept of Transportation is rolling back Biden-era plans to require automakers to increase their fleet’s mileage performance. Rather than the goal of 50.4 mpg, the new rules will settle for 34.9 mpg by 2031. The White House claims this may save you $1,300 on the cost of a new car.



But savings on the sticker price won’t be free. Because the new cars won’t get the targeted mileage improvements, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates you’ll spend $1,624 more for gas over the life of your vehicle.
By the way, according to the industry ‘bible,’ Kelley Blue Book, the average new vehicle in the U.S. now costs $50,089, up almost 2% in one year.
That will puts new vehicle buyers in Connecticut into a higher tax bracket: 7.75% sales tax for “luxury cars” vs the usual 6.35%, meaning the average new set of wheels in Connecticut will now, legally, be a luxury.
Another CT highway worker death: For the second time in two years a Connecticut Department of Transportation highway worker has been killed doing his job. Sixty-year-old Elvin Hernandez was doing road maintenance on I-95 when he was hit by a car that was driving on the grass on the right shoulder near exit 20.

Elvin Hernandez, the CDOT highway worker killed by an out-of-control motorist. Credit: CTDOT

The driver of that car, Edward Myers, also age 60, was arrested and admitted to officers he’d just used heroin. Myers was convicted of driving under the influence this past April and has been on probation. He’s now being held on $2 million bond, charged with manslaughter.
Working alongside our highways with cars zooming by at high speed is a challenging and dangerous job. Recent efforts at placing speed cameras in work zones have seen some success. A pilot test for eight months in 2023 saw 24,900 warning notices issued to drivers, but only 750 violations. During testing this spring cameras clocked 8.4 million cars passing the work zones, 1.36 million of them exceeding the speed limit. More than 150 drivers were clocked in excess of 100 mph.
Tariffs and new rail cars: Metro-North parent MTA (the Metropolitan Transportation Authority) plans to spend $23 billion on new rail cars, subway cars and buses. But the price tag is being inflated by $1 billion due to new tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on imported components. That’s enough money to buy 150 Long Island Railroad train cars, almost 1,000 buses or more than 250 subway cars.
The White House tariffs on imported railroad gear “will not result in a [domestic U.S.] railcar manufacturing boom; it will only raise costs for transit agencies at a time when other construction costs are skyrocketing” the MTA board was told this week.
That’s code for eventually “higher fares.”
Brightline: As I predicted weeks ago, this modern, stylish, for-profit passenger railroad in Florida has filed for bankruptcy.
Ridership and fares are not growing as fast as hoped… revenue is less than half of what was predicted… so the railroad has had to restructure $2.5 billion in debt.
So much for the free market saving passenger rail, fueled by junk bonds.
Meanwhile, the railroad’s trains between Miami and Orlando will keep running. However, Brightline’s plan for a high-speed line from Southern California to Las Vegas is already behind schedule and still hunting for money.
