title: Area Trump apologists lecture community on ‘character’
description: A pregnant woman shot dead in a parking lot. What a horrible tragedy. And if you’re the political professionals trying to reelect Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, what a fabulous campaign issue. Lombardo’s campaign and allied PACs and organizations have been hammering Lombardo’s Democratic opponent, Attorney General Aaron Ford, for sponsoring a pardon hearing a[...]
text:
President Donald Trump and character witness Joe Lombardo. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)A pregnant woman shot dead in a parking lot. What a horrible tragedy.
And if you’re the political professionals trying to reelect Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, what a fabulous campaign issue.
Lombardo’s campaign and allied PACs and organizations have been hammering Lombardo’s Democratic opponent, Attorney General Aaron Ford, for sponsoring a pardon hearing application for Norman Smith.
Smith had been initially charged with murder with a deadly weapon in the death of Tineshea Adams in 2015. According to the Review-Journal’s coverage of the case, the scene involved what the police report described as “multiple people,” and Smith’s attorney, assisted by surveillance video, argued during Smith’s trial that the gunshot that killed Adams was unintentional. Smith was ultimately convicted of voluntary manslaughter.
By the time he was convicted in 2018, Smith was already incarcerated for convictions connected to his participation with a half dozen other people in a spree of robberies and assaults earlier in 2015 (again according to the R-J). 
Now that Lombardo’s campaign and its organizational PACs and allies are focusing so much attention on the matter, Smith’s multiple sentences have helped create competing interpretations of which sentences were up for pardoning.  
KLAS took a good swing at trying to unpack the details: Ford’s office contends the pardon was about the robbery charges, not the manslaughter conviction. Smith’s attorney argued in the parole application that Smith had already served the minimum 8 years on the manslaughter sentence. The Department of Corrections disagrees.
There’s a lot going on, you see, and the matter isn’t as plain and simple as Lombardo’s campaign and its allies want voters to think.
That said, Ford’s explanations have been opaque, which is not a preferred behavior from a politician but an exceedingly common one.
Meanwhile, it would be nice — refreshing, even — to believe Lombardo and his campaign affiliates are sincerely upset by Ford signing an an application for a state board to hear an argument for a pardon.
Alas, the relish of their enthusiasm for the issue casts doubt on the genuineness of their disapprobation.
An ad by the Lombardo-supporting Better Nevada PAC, evidently an organization that is not shy about racist tropes, hammers Ford on the pardon issue by running pictures of Black men in scary poses and a voiceover of what sounds like a white suburban mom saying things like “gruesomely gunned down” and “gang member” and “siding with criminals.” 
Familiarity with ads nationwide would be required to guess which Republican race-baiting campaign ad will win the 2026 election cycle’s Willie Horton sweepstakes, but the entry by the pro-Lombardo PAC must be a strong contender.
And running ads like that is a lot easier than defending Trump’s economy.
But might we all take a moment to note that what we have here is Joe Lombardo, a defender of and apologist for Donald Trump, asking the Nevada voting public to be outraged over the prospect of a convicted criminal getting a pardon?
The star of Lombard’s 2022 campaign for governor was the one he wore on his sheriff’s uniform in illegal campaign ads. Brave, strong, straight-shootin’ lawman of the West is Lombardo’s assiduously cultivated political brand.
Trump indiscriminately pardoned 1,600 people who stormed the Capitol, including those who had been convicted of violent crimes against Lombardo’s fellow law enforcement professionals (more than 140 of whom were injured in the insurrection and five of whom would end up dead). Asked at the time about Trump’s pardons of the January 6 rioters, Lombardo failed to respond.
Web searching reveals no evidence that the former sheriff has muttered a public peep about those reckless and disgusting pardons ever since. Nor is there a readily available trace of Lombardo commenting on any of Trump’s multiple pardons of violent drug traffickers, both foreign and domestic, let alone Trump’s many, many pardons of grifters, cronies, conmen, and general purpose skanks, often in a pay-to-play fashion.
When Lombardo, like good little obedient Republicans from coast to coast, endorsed Trump for president in 2024, Trump had already been found liable of sexual abuse by one jury, and found guilty of 34 felonies by another for covering up hush money payments to a porn star. And four years earlier, in the course of attempting to overthrow the U.S. Constitution and steal an election, Trump had tried to nullify the majority of ballots cast by Nevada voters.
Lombardo’s regard for law and order can be situational. 
So voters can be forgiven for assuming Lombardo’s concern about Ford sponsoring someone’s application for a pardon hearing is not driven by Lombardo’s devotion to law and order, but pure politics.
Hoping to attract more attention to what it obviously feels is a much more important issue than affordability, Lombardo’s campaign in a press release Wednesday declared Ford’s purported sins with respect to a pardon application reflect Ford’s “character.”
You know what else reflects a politician’s character? Bowing before and sucking up to the most venal, corrupt, and immoral president in U.S. history.
If Lombardo agrees with his own campaign’s assertion that an elected official’s character is a matter of such crucial concern, he should take a good look at the president he folds for on command. And for that matter, a mirror.
And if voters decide Ford signing an application for a pardon hearing is a deal breaker, that’s their business. But they should keep in mind that the Lombardo campaign and its PACs and allies can be deliberately unreliable sources.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Who should bear the cost of University of Minnesota’s budget problems?
description: In the University of Minnesota’s announcement of $225 million in budget cuts over two years beginning in July 2027, President Rebecca Cunningham described the decision as an “institutional inflection point.” The financial pressures facing the university are real, but who bears the greatest costs remains a choice. Will Cunningham and the Board of Regents cont[...]
text:
University of Minnesota students leave Pioneer Hall in November 2022. (Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)In the University of Minnesota’s announcement of $225 million in budget cuts over two years beginning in July 2027, President Rebecca Cunningham described the decision as an “institutional inflection point.”
The financial pressures facing the university are real, but who bears the greatest costs remains a choice. Will Cunningham and the Board of Regents continue placing that burden on students, staff and faculty, or pursue solutions advancing the land-grant mission by empowering Minnesota’s working families?
While the scale of these cuts is staggering, faculty, staff and students are accustomed to austerity budgets expecting them to do more with less. 
In July, the University announced higher employee health costs beginning in January 2027, the same day the regents extended Cunningham’s contract and added up to $1.48 million in retirement contributions through 2031. These decisions followed two years of budget cuts and tuition hikes that demanded sacrifice from students and workers while the University created a new vice presidency. It also committed $15 million over five years to a marketing contract that produced the discarded “Leave a Future” slogan.
The U’s budget tables for 2025 show $138.2 million in consulting and professional services spending from nonsponsored funds — meaning the operating budget, nothing tied to external funding like federal research grants. 
A Star Tribune analysis found “academic administrative” headcount grew 32% from 2017 to 2025, compared with 6% for faculty, while its payroll share rose from 11% to 13% as faculty’s fell from 29% to 27%. Because that category includes research, student services and technology, the numbers are not proof of waste. But they raise the question: Why is sacrifice concentrated elsewhere?
We have little reason to expect the coming budget cycles to be different under Cunningham and the Board of Regents’ leadership. 
The Morris campus, my alma mater, has already endured years of cuts to academic programs and staffing. More cuts would undermine efforts to increase enrollment while reducing the value Morris offers. Although Morris reports the lowest average student debt in the university system, that means less if cuts eliminate the programs students came to study, push professors to seek better pay elsewhere and leave faculty stretched too thin to offer the learning experience students deserve.
But this does not have to be how Cunningham and the Board of Regents “leave a future” for Minnesota’s working families.
In the announcement, Cunningham promised to restructure the university’s budgeting process to allow broader input in financial decisions. (Transparency would help, too: The budget is far too opaque for average people to examine.) 
University leadership has a responsibility to establish a genuinely democratic process, giving Minnesotans a voice through sharing real deliberation, rather than lip service. As a former student body president, I am familiar with the administration’s tendency to invite consultation without meaningfully sharing power. This moment calls for the University to forgo that pattern and treat people’s voices as more than a box to check.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The moment also calls upon university leadership to consider how it shares in our sacrifices by reining in their worst excesses. While it may not be enough to offset the costs of the forthcoming cuts, it would be meaningful if Cunningham paused spending on exorbitant consultant contracts, froze hiring of new senior leadership positions, or asked the university’s highest-paid executives — herself included — to accept temporary pay cuts before asking others to sacrifice even more. 
Public university presidents have set a precedent of accepting pay cuts in similar moments of financial crisis. Even a modest reduction would demonstrate that university leadership is committed to working families and bearing some of the burden being asked of us.
I came to the University of Minnesota from the Rosebud Indian Reservation in 2019. Growing up in a community devastated by poverty, pursuing a college education and using it to make positive change was my greatest dream. My Morris experience made that dream real and even inspired me to continue my education at the U’s Humphrey School of Public Affairs. I still believe in the opportunity of higher education, I still believe in the U, and I share Cunningham’s hope these cuts will create a sense of mission and collective purpose.
But collective purpose cannot be imposed from the top down, and sacrifice cannot always be demanded from the bottom up. 
University leadership has a choice: continue down the familiar path of austerity, or build a future worthy of the working families this university exists to serve.

name: Delaware
title: Back after 1,076 days, Wahkeem Roman Returns to the Blue Hens’ Huddle
description: University of Delaware sixth year offensive lineman, Wahkeem Roman, played his first game as a Blue Hen on September 3 against Merrimack, returning to play after two missed seasons due to injury.   NEWARK, DE — UD’s opening game against Merrimack drew over 17,000 fans into Delaware Stadium. The venue was filled with life, excitement, and hope for a new ... R[...]
text:
Blue Hen offensive lineman Wahkeem Roman (65) gets ready to block during his first game as a Blue Hen. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
University of Delaware sixth year offensive lineman, Wahkeem Roman, played his first game as a Blue Hen on September 3 against Merrimack, returning to play after two missed seasons due to injury.
 
NEWARK, DE — UD’s opening game against Merrimack drew over 17,000 fans into Delaware Stadium. The venue was filled with life, excitement, and hope for a new football season after a successful first at the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) level. It’s an environment that any first time Blue Hen could admire while stepping between the white lines for the first time.
Wahkeem Roman had every reason to soak in his surroundings. He experienced multiple home openers stuck on the sidelines during his first two seasons in the blue and gold. This was his first opportunity to truly experience the environment while donning the pads and standing amongst his fellow lineman in the huddle. 
Yet, all his focus was trained on one thing. Playing the game he loves for the first time in over 1,000 days.
“I was just so locked in on the game like at that point, I didn’t even realize like I was coming back from an injury,” Roman said. 
Roman joined the University of Delaware football program before the 2024 season. His transfer was unique. 
Roman attended Notre Dame College located in South Euclid, Ohio, before the former division two school was shut down in the spring of 2024. The other unique variable to Roman’s transfer, an injury to his right knee that affected his ACL, MCL and PCL. 
The school closure left Roman without many other options other than entering the transfer portal and the injury made him unsure if any program would take a chance on him, but Roman said he received offers from programs at both the FBS and Football Championship Subdivision (FCS) levels.  
The Blue Hens liked what they saw on the limited amount of film Roman had coming into the portal — Roman started four games for Notre Dame College during the 2023 season — said Blue Hen offensive line coach and run game coordinator, Chris Rogers. Rogers and the coaching staff felt like he fit their style of football and would be successful in their system. Off the field, coach Rogers knew that he had the character and fortitude to return from the injury.
“In this business you evaluate people as much or more than you evaluate people as players, and so on film he was a really good player, but also … I really liked the person,” Rogers said. “He said the right things. You could tell he wanted to be developed, you could tell football mattered to him, you could tell this was important, you could tell being successful in college was important, and so like a person who’s got all those traits, obviously, you know, they’re gonna battle they’re way back from an injury and be successful after that.”
Roman blocks against Virginia defensive end Evan Ward during the Blue Hens’ road game against the Cavaliers. Photo Credit: University of Delaware Football.
Roman said the program made him feel like family and accepted him from the moment he arrived. With that comfortability and access to better training resources, he began attacking the rehabilitation process alongside Delaware’s training staff. While his teammates were competing in summer workouts, Roman was in the training room working steadily to improve and strengthen his right leg.
“First we’ll be trying to get my quad to fire, and next week we’ll try to like get my extension all over there and then after all that, maybe I’ll get back walking [on] the treadmill,” Roman said. “It was just week by week, we had a plan and a progress, and it was good.”
Roman essentially had to start the rehab process from square one when he transferred in. The UD training staff discovered that while Roman thought he was ahead in his rehab, it turned out he was actually a little behind in the process. 
“I had to catch all the way up and basically start from the beginning, and that was a real slow process, and it was like killer because, … you just want to get back on the field and want to be like a part of the team, you know,” Roman said.
Roman’s recovery cost him the full 2024 season — UD’s last in FCS football — and an injury to the same ACL in the spring of 2025 required him to miss the full 2025 season— UD’s first in FBS football.
“He walked in my office and, you know, I felt like I saw a tear fall down his cheek, and in 15 seconds, I watched that same tear roll back up his cheek and into his eye and it lit a fire under him,” Rogers said. 
Roman started the rehab process again, this time with lessons learned from the first time around.
“That’s what I learned the second time around, to really just focus on getting my body back and not rush anything,” Roman said. “My footwork and everything always comes back, it’s just the strengthening that you gotta get back.”
Roman was cleared to play a week into the 2026 spring session. He learned to trust his body to perform at an elite level like it had before, a skill Roman credits to the work of UD’s athletic training staff and former football head athletic trainer, Annie Stock, who helped him rebuild that confidence in himself and his body. 
“She would always instill confidence into me like, ‘you’ve done this before, it’s not anything you can’t do, I wouldn’t have you doing it if I didn’t believe in you to do it’ and you just sit back and think like, well, yeah, she doesn’t want me to get hurt again, so obviously I should be good enough to do this,” Roman said. 
His first one on one rep in spring practice cemented his confidence in his body’s ability to return to its prior elite level. 
“I anchored on a bull rush and I was like ‘oh yeah, this feels good. We’re good to go’,” Roman said.
The Elizabeth, New Jersey, native has played in two games for the Blue Hens this season. His last appearance came in the Blue Hen’s most recent game against Virginia that closed out their non-conference schedule. It was his first chance to play on a Power 4 field against Power 4 competition. 
It’s a cool experience for a player whose career embarked on a whirlwind of a journey. A journey that saw him overcome adversity, achieve academic success (Wahkeem earned his bachelor’s degree in communications from the University of Delaware in May) and become a leader for the younger players in the offensive line room.
Wahkeem Roman lines up on the left side of the offensive line against Merrimack. This was his first time playing for the Blue Hens since transferring into the program during the spring of 2024. Photo Credit: University of Delaware Football.
“Giving him a hug before the [Merrimack] game was a big moment and I think he deserves that. I tell him all the time I’m thankful I got in the car and drove to go see him and meet him and recruit him,” coach Rogers said. “I’m thankful to be his football coach.”
As Wahkeem completed his first drive as a Blue Hen and walked to the sideline, he said all he remembers is his teammates’ excitement for him. The reality of the moment still hadn’t settled in. There was still an opponent on the field, a game to win and a job to get done. 
The Blue Hens defeated Merrimack, 42-7. The team was heading back into the locker room — celebrating — but Roman and his teammate Chandler Telfaire needed to return to the field. They forgot a pair of gloves. 
It was at that moment, Wahkeem Roman looked around Delaware stadium and fully took in where his 1,076 day journey led him.
“I was just like wow, I really just came back and played in this stadium. It was a surreal feeling.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Trump’s immigration sweeps leave southwest Kansas communities looking for way forward
description: DODGE CITY — Southwest Kansas communities reeling from President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown — which included random stops to check status — are looking for ways to recover as fear continues to grip the area’s large Hispanic population.  Restaurants closed, motel managers cancelled reservations and the area’s large beef processing facilities shorten[...]
text:
Dodge City protesters gather on Sept. 25, 2026, outside U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann's office, chanting "Tracey Mann, where are you? We need you?" They were protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)DODGE CITY — Southwest Kansas communities reeling from President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown — which included random stops to check status — are looking for ways to recover as fear continues to grip the area’s large Hispanic population. 
Restaurants closed, motel managers cancelled reservations and the area’s large beef processing facilities shortened or called off shifts last week as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers rushed in and immigrant employees didn’t show up for work. 
Breanna Rutschman, a Dodge City second grade teacher, said seven of her 20 students were absent the day the agents arrived. The next day, just eight students showed up. Other classrooms in the school were largely empty.
“They’re here to better their situation and improve the lives of their children, and they’re just hardworking and they’re caring and they’re human,” she said. “What’s happening is so inhumane and so cruel, and it’s unnecessary. It’s absolutely unnecessary.”
ICE agents arrived in the area Sept. 22, focusing immigration checks in Dodge City, Liberal and Garden City. The federal government reported making more than 100 arrests. Trump’s Department of Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin said through news releases that agents were arresting only “heinous criminals”
But on a list including murderers, rapists, and drug traffickers he added “illegal aliens with final orders of removal.” Mullin also said ICE agents, who work for Homeland Security, are not arresting people at worksites.
Local officials and advocates say that’s not what happened.
“It wasn’t just criminals, because I’ve been in contact with several schools, and I’ve been in contact with the families directly,” said Janeth Vazquez, vice mayor of Liberal. “The majority of these families did not have any criminal history. These were hardworking, humble, genuine, good people in our communities.” 
Census data shows that Liberal, Dodge City and Garden City have populations ranging from 55% to 69% Hispanic or Latino.
As word of ICE’s presence spread, Vazquez said, Liberal became a “ghost town,” as people hid. 
Federal officers arrested people after demanding proof of immigration status during traffic stops and from employees entering beef processing plants, and based on outstanding warrants, Vazaquez said.
“I’m not just talking about undocumented people. I’m talking about U.S. citizens as well,” she said. “They were racially profiling people and targeting people of color, and so all of those stories were shared across social media. People were terrified to leave their homes.”
 
Volunteers Aquilino Reyes (left), Amy Soberanes (center) and Anna Meyer load supplies on Sept. 24, 2026, that were donated to Dodge City immigrants afraid to leave their homes while U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were in town. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Helping out
Amy Soberanes owns a small Dodge City shop selling juices and lattes. But since the ICE arrests she has another job: organizing a relief network to deliver food and other essentials to immigrants in hiding.
The front porch of Soberanes’ business was covered with donations in the days after the immigration searches. She gathered a team of driver-volunteers who go to homes to drop off diapers, baby formula, toilet paper and groceries, a community practice employed in Minneapolis, Los Angeles and other cities when ICE arrived. 
The volunteers are careful, Soberanes said. Drivers switch routes and cars to avoid detection, and they write addresses on notebook paper and carry a water bottle so they can drop the paper in the water and obscure the addresses should they be stopped by authorities. 
Last week, her phone rang constantly as she juggled boxes of diapers, bags of fruit and rolls of toilet paper.
“I have not slept the past three days,” she said Friday. “We have been out delivering food until midnight, and then getting up in the morning at 4 a.m. and delivering food before (ICE is) active from 8 a.m. to probably 6 p.m.”
Soberanes nonetheless said she was heartened by everyone who volunteered to help. Even cancellation of a long-planned Hispanic community event, the Pachanga en la Plaza, had a bright side, she said.  
“What we are doing now is we have turned all the free food we were going to give out for the event, all the money we had gotten for it, and we are now donating it to the families,” Soberanes said.
 
Hurting, in hiding
In a small house, a family of seven crowded the living room last week, scared to leave and relying on donations dropped off by Soberanes. 
A young woman, whom Kansas Reflector is not identifying because of her fear that ICE may retaliate against her and her family, cuddled her newborn son as she talked about her husband’s detention by ICE days earlier. 
On Sept. 23, the woman and her husband were on the way home from the hospital with their newborn baby, she said in Spanish, speaking with help of a translator. Their doctor warned the couple to be careful as they traveled home because it was “dangerous” out there. 
Despite precautions, they were stopped by ICE, and her husband was detained.
“The agents did have some mercy, but it was very little,” the woman said. “He let my kid and me go. One thing I am incredibly grateful for is that I am with my three kids here at home.”
The arrest happened near the couple’s house, she said, where her 4-year-old son came outside and saw her husband taken away. 
“They didn’t care about my husband, and they just took him. I’m incredibly sad,” she said. Her husband immigrated to the United States with a work permit, but it wasn’t renewed. 
“He appealed his case,” the woman said. “He did everything that was required of him. He came here legally. He did everything. They just didn’t renew it.”
An appeals court upheld a lower court’s decision that asylum and an application for protection under the Convention Against Torture were not appropriate for him, court records confirm. The court decided that the man’s refusal to join criminal gangs in Guatemala was not sufficient to show his life was endangered, and that his race didn’t play a role in his fear of specific “actors” in his birth country. 
“His lawyer at the time told him just stay where you’re at and just don’t do anything,” the woman said. “So he didn’t know what to do. We feel like that lawyer didn’t help us at all that time, but we didn’t know much at the moment, so we just let it go.” 
The woman said she spoke on the phone to her husband days after agents took him. He said he was being held in San Diego but expected to be deported to Guatemala.
She said she doesn’t see how she can return to Guatemala. 
“I can’t because of my kids. I need to take care of my kids. They have a future here,” she said. “In Guatemala, there is no future. We don’t have a house there. We don’t have anything.”
The couple’s current attorney said she can’t help anymore because she can’t get in contact with the husband, the woman said. 
The young woman dissolved into quiet tears when she talked about her husband. “He hasn’t done anything. He doesn’t drink. He plays in the church band. These were the last words that he told me: ‘Take care of yourself. Take care of our kids.’”
Volunteers, including three attorneys who are working pro bono with southwest Kansas immigrants, will coordinate with the man to help him apply to return, Soberanes said. The family was unsure if he signed a stipulation agreement while in detention, a form commonly used with immigrant detainees in which they agree to be deported without going through immigration court, according to the National Immigration Project. 
The man was the breadwinner for his family of seven, which includes his wife and their three children, his own mother, and his younger brother, who is deaf. 
 
Protesters in downtown Dodge City on Sept. 24, 2026, protest the presence of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Protesting ICE
In response to ICE’s presence, hundreds of people lined Dodge City’s signature downtown plaza with its life-sized bronze Texas longhorn steer on Sept. 24, waving flags from Mexico, Guatemala and the United States.
They carried signs urging kindness and cursing ICE. 
The following day, protesters marched from Wright Park to U.S. Republican Rep. Tracey Mann’s Dodge City office, where the doors were locked before the demonstrators arrived. Mann represents Kansas’ vast 1st Congressional District, which stretches some 400 miles east to west, from Lawrence to the border with Colorado.
Mann did not answer Kansas Reflector questions submitted by email about why the office was closed or whether he was concerned by disruptions to Kansas businesses. 
“Federal law enforcement has a responsibility to enforce our immigration laws and help keep our communities safe,” Mann said in an emailed statement. “I also recognize the disruption the operation caused for communities across the Big First. When possible, federal authorities should coordinate with local law enforcement so operations can be carried out safely.”
 
Ana Sanchez Ortiz shares the story of her mother, who was taken by U.S. Immigration and Customs enforcement agents on Sept. 23, 2026, in Dodge City. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Complications of gaining citizenship
Not all iof those n southwest Kansas are sympathetic about the ICE raids. 
Residents commented under social media posts telling immigrants to simply file paperwork to gain legal status or leave, and thanking ICE for their work, even as others mourned families torn apart.
But attaining citizenship isn’t as easy as it may sound. 
In 2011, Ana Sanchez Ortiz’s stepfather petitioned for her, along with her siblings and mother, to become U.S. citizens. 
Fifteen years later, Sanchez Ortiz’s mother still isn’t a citizen, and on Sept. 23, she was detained. That was despite checking in for years with ICE, holding a job at National Beef Packing Co. and staying out of trouble, Sanchez Ortiz said.
Sanchez Ortiz, a senior branch manager at a Dodge City bank, hesitated at first to speak out, fearful of drawing attention. 
But frantic family members couldn’t find her mother in the federal detention system for several days, she said. Her mother is diabetic and has high blood pressure, and although Sanchez Ortiz’s sister rushed her medications to the local jail, ICE agents wouldn’t give it to her mother. 
The family now know their mother is being detained in California, and they have traveled there to try to help her, Sanchez Ortiz said. 
“We have done everything the right way. She’s been here since she was 16 years old,” Sanchez Ortiz said. “She went to high school here. She started her family here.”
Because she came to the country when she was 4 years old, Sanchez Ortiz became a citizen through the DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, program. This Obama-era immigration policy allows certain immigrants who were brought to the United States as children to receive renewable two-year work permits
She renewed her DACA application six times before she could apply for the separate status of legal residency, which she received when she was a freshman in high school. But it wasn’t until she was 31 years old that she became a citizen, Sanchez Ortiz said.
 
Julysa Barraza, a local activist, explains a petition for the SEAL Act, which would create a clear path for immigrants to become U.S. citizens, during a rally on Sept. 24, 2026, in Dodge City. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Looking for a solution
Zac Carlton owns a construction company in Dodge City, and he said friends were “gutted” by ICE activities last week. Everyone in the area knows someone who is not here legally, he said. 
“I’ve talked to multiple contractors and subcontractors, and everybody was laying low last week, and no work was getting done,” he said. “Now this week, people are trying to figure out how to recover. It has put a strain on, obviously, the families that were affected by the sweep, and then the employers.”
Western Kansas needs immigrants to support construction, agriculture and other businesses, Carlton said. Finding workers is already an issue in those industries, he said, and will continue to be so. 
Carlton looked at past immigration laws and policies and is circulating a petition to promote the SEAL Act, which stands for secure, earned, accountable and lawful, he said. 
Immigration reform bills have failed multiple times in the past, he said, but he’s hopeful politicians will pay attention after what happened in Kansas. 
Vazquez has been fighting the battle Carlton is attempting for about 15 years, traveling to Washington, D.C., to advocate for immigration changes. She began when her father was deported right as she started college as a teenager. Five years ago, she became a Liberal city commissioner, the first Latina in the position.
What happened in Southwest Kansas last week will reverberate across the nation because of the effects on the beef supply, she said. Industry groups raised concerns that employees who skipped work at beef processing facilities for fear of encountering ICE could contribute to slowed production and higher prices. 
“This whole operation just truly put an impact on our economy, and everybody in Southwest Kansas is going to suffer,” Vazquez said, “not just the undocumented population.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan lawmakers, state leaders announce $89M for Detroit and Kalamazoo River cleanup
description: DETROIT — Overcast skies and a sprinkling of rain that fell over Sunset Point on Belle Isle on Thursday afternoon failed to dim the excitement from government officials as Gov. Gretchen joined the heads of the Department of Natural Resources and the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to announce a substantial investment into […]
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announces $89 million in funding to clean up the Detroit and Kalamazoo rivers during an event on Belle Isle, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — Overcast skies and a sprinkling of rain that fell over Sunset Point on Belle Isle on Thursday afternoon failed to dim the excitement from government officials as Gov. Gretchen joined the heads of the Department of Natural Resources and the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to announce a substantial investment into the cleanup of two major waterways.
Alongside EGLE Director Phil Roos and DNR Director Scott Bowen, Whitmer unveiled the state’s Reclaim the Rivers initiative, which is committing $89 million in environmental settlement funds for the clean up and restoration of the Detroit and Kalamazoo rivers.
“This is a big deal,” Whitmer said during the announcement in Detroit. “Together, we will continue our work to protect wildlife, reduce pollution, and ensure every Michigander can enjoy beautiful places just like this all across our great state, our state is defined by water. It’s who we are, and it’s up to us to protect it, all of it, from our Great Lakes to our local rivers.”
The two bodies of water each carry their own legacy of industrial pollution, with Superfund sites — some of the most contaminated areas in the nation — located on each waterway. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Of the $89 million investment stemming from environmental settlement dollars, $50 million will be dedicated to cleaning up polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs, in the Detroit River. The chemicals were used in manufacturing until 1979 and have been tied to several harmful health effects including cancer, harm to the immune system and neurological effects.
Roos explained that the $50 million would be used to secure hundreds of millions in additional dollars from the federal government and the private sector to help cover the cost of cleanup.
Another $25 million will be used for river restoration initiatives in the Kalamazoo River, while the remaining $14 million will be put into a strategic fund for river restoration projects across the state, including dam removal, wetland restoration and habitat improvements.
Roos emphasized that the cleanup initiatives would not start from scratch, but would rather build upon the efforts of federal agencies, tribal governments, state employees, community members and leaders, as well as members of the private sector and philanthropic organizations.
Roos pointed to the initiative as a hallmark of Whitmer’s environmental work during her time as governor, and noted that the effort reflects their shared belief that environmental protections and economic opportunities are not opposed and can work in tandem.
“This project’s about certainly cleaning up PCBs and other contaminants, but it’s a lot more than that,” Roos said. “It’s about truly reclaiming, and transforming our rivers.”
Economic growth doesn’t just relate to jobs, Roos said — it’s about people looking to stay and build their lives in Michigan. Having beautiful places to swim, paddle and play is part of that equation, Roos added.
“That’s what we are building here with this Reclaim the Rivers initiative,” he said. “At the end of the day, the work of our agency is about people, protecting public health, ensuring clean water, creating healthier communities, and improving quality of life.”
U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) discusses efforts to remedy industrial pollution in the Detroit River, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) also attended the announcement. Dingell noted that while the Detroit River supported the industries that built the state’s middle class, that same legacy has also left behind pollution that officials have spent decades trying to clean up. 
“We’ve made tremendous progress, and we’re celebrating that, but there’s still a lot of work ahead,” Dingell said. “Our goal must be more than cleaning up the pollution of the past. It must be ensuring that every Michigan family can enjoy these rivers for generations to come.”
Detroit City Councilmember Scott Benson spoke to reporters following the announcement, and said that the cleanup for the Detroit River carries a price tag of roughly $1 billion. Benson called the newly announced investment as an incremental investment toward getting the historical contaminants out of the river.
“One bite at a time, that’s how you eat the elephant,” Benson said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Outgoing assemblymember takes on lieutenant governor
description: Republican Lieutenant Gov. Stravos Anthony is looking to defend his seat against Democratic challenger Sandra Jauregui at a time when Democrats are feeling optimistic about their chances of flipping control of statewide seats. In Nevada, the post is largely ceremonial with little day-to-day statutory authority – but if the sitting governor dies, resigns or i[...]
text:
Sandra Jauregui, Stavros Anthony. (Candidate photos)Republican Lieutenant Gov. Stravos Anthony is looking to defend his seat against Democratic challenger Sandra Jauregui at a time when Democrats are feeling optimistic about their chances of flipping control of statewide seats.
In Nevada, the post is largely ceremonial with little day-to-day statutory authority – but if the sitting governor dies, resigns or is removed from office, the lieutenant governor is the first in line to lead the state.
That scenario has not played out since 1989 when Bob Miller took the job after Gov. Richard Bryan had been elected to the U.S. Senate. Before that, a lieutenant governor hadn’t assumed the duties of governor since 1945, when Vail Pittman became governor after Gov. Edward Carville was appointed to fill a vacant U.S. Senate seat.
The more immediate duties of lieutenant governor — which commands an annual salary of $63,648 — include presiding over the state Senate, where they can cast tie-breaking votes, although opportunities to do that are exceedingly rare since the Nevada Senate has an odd number of members. The lieutenant governor also  leads commissions on tourism and outdoor recreation, and has a seat on several state boards.
Anthony’s newly created Task Force to Protect Women’s Sports has been at the center of his campaign for reelection. His only campaign ad touts his efforts to ban transgender athletes from women’s sports during his first term. 
His campaign suggested his task force led to the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association in April 2025 approving a policy requiring high school students to play in sport divisions that align with the sex listed on their original birth certificate.
He sued the Nevada Commission on Ethics in July over their ruling that he violated state ethics laws by using state resources to promote the task force.
Throughout her campaign, Jauregui has criticized Anthony over those ethics violations and accused him of neglecting his statutory duties as chair of the Nevada Commission on Tourism. 
“He’s falling short in every aspect of the job. He’s done nothing to help Nevada families. He’s done nothing to fulfill his constitutional and statutory assigned duty. Tourism is down on his watch. The only thing the current lieutenant governor has done is mount up ethics violations,” Jauregui told the Nevada Current in May.
Anthony did not respond to multiple requests for an interview. The Nevada Current interviewed Jauregui in May during the Democratic primary. 
Tourism and outdoor recreation
The lieutenant governor serves as the chair of the Nevada Commission on Tourism and the Advisory Board on Outdoor Recreation. 
Tourism in Nevada has experienced a significant downturn, a product of inflationary pressures brought on by tariffs and the Iran war, and Donald Trump’s acrimonious behavior with other nations, including Canada — long the largest source of international visitors to Las Vegas. Anthony’s website says he “helped lead a remarkable, post-pandemic rebound in our state’s leading economic industry.” 
On his website, Anthony acknowledged recent economic headwinds have impacted the state’s gaming and resort corridors, but said he believes Nevada “will finish the year on pace for continued growth while rural tourism and outdoor recreation remain resilient.”
Jauregui laid part of the blame for tourism decline on President Donald Trump’s rhetoric and tariff policies. 
“Our current lieutenant governor is doing nothing to stand up to this current administration to fight back on the policies that are actively harming Nevada. We have lost tourism from two of our biggest visiting countries, Canada and Mexico,” Jauregui said.
Jauregui said she aims to expand tourism beyond the Strip, downtown Reno, and Lake Tahoe. That work would include doing more to promote eco-tourism in the state, including Nevada’s dark skies week, Jauregui said.
Promoting eco-tourism would attract more people to rural Nevada and diversify the state’s tourism economy beyond gaming and entertainment in Reno and Las Vegas, said Jauregui. 
Transportation
The lieutenant governor serves as the vice chair of the Board of Transportation.
When it comes to transportation, Anthony has largely focused on eliminating high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes across the state. Since taking office, he’s worked with the Board of the Nevada Department of Transportation to limit operating hours for HOV lanes, and helped initiate a two-year study with the federal government to examine HOV lanes in certain areas.
Jauregui said if elected, she would prioritize working with local transportation authorities to understand their unique needs, including removing regulatory red tape to speed up infrastructure projects and create jobs. 
Economic development 
Nevada policy for attracting businesses and industry relies on providing tax abatements, credits, and other incentives to business, which are reviewed and approved by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development (GOED). The lieutenant governor serves as one of 11 voting members on that board. 
Anthony told the Fernley Reporter that tax abatements can have a negative impact on the state through loss of tax revenue, but have more positive impact on local government by expanding the local tax base. 
Jauregui said Nevada should ensure that any company applying for tax abatements are “good corporate citizens” that support the community with good paying jobs. For data centers, Jauregui said tax abatements should be determined based on whether they are “sustaining their own energy and water systems” and “creating their own capacity.”
Jauregui said she also supports Nevada’s Assembly Joint Resolution 8, which would amend the Nevada State Constitution to establish a dedicated business court. She said the court would go a long way to attract businesses to the state beyond tax abatements.
Bipartisanship
Nevada is one of 17 U.S. states that independently elect their lieutenant governor, separate from the governor. The setup gives Nevada the opportunity to elect a governor and lieutenant governor from different political parties. 
Jauregui said she has a proven track record of working with Lombardo as an Assembly member. She pointed to her work as the lead legislator on Lombardo’s housing bill, Assembly Bill 540. 
“When it comes to working on policies that are in the best interest of Nevada families, I’m willing to work with anyone to get those policies across to the finish line, and I’ve proven that. I’ve done that in the legislature,” Jauregui said in May. 
Anthony has a history of working in nonpartisan roles. He represented Ward 4 on the Las Vegas City Council from 2009 to 2022, where he also served as the Mayor pro tempore for several years. He also previously served on the Nevada System of Higher Education’s Board of Regents from 2003-2009.

name: Nevada Current
title: Prosecutor seeks to oust judge from Clark County District Court
description: Judge Jennifer Schwartz, who is wrapping up her first term on the bench, faces a reelection challenge from prosecutor Jacob Villani in Clark County District Court Department 17.  Schwartz is a lifelong Las Vegan and graduate of UNLV’s Boyd School of Law. She began her career as a law clerk for Judge Michael Cherry, who […]
text:
Jacob Villani, Jennifer Schwartz. (Campaign photos)Judge Jennifer Schwartz, who is wrapping up her first term on the bench, faces a reelection challenge from prosecutor Jacob Villani in Clark County District Court Department 17. 
Schwartz is a lifelong Las Vegan and graduate of UNLV’s Boyd School of Law. She began her career as a law clerk for Judge Michael Cherry, who presided over civil and criminal cases at the time. Schwartz also served as a public defender before her election to the bench. 
Schwartz presides over a split docket. She says she gained experience in civil practice while working for a law firm before joining the public defender. 
Still, she says, it took some studying to get up to speed. “Civil law is complicated, and I hadn’t done it in so long.”
Schwartz says she was briefly challenged to discard her defense bias upon taking the bench. 
“I view it as I am the neutral arbitrator, and instead of advocating for a particular side, I get to truly appreciate the entire case from all perspectives,” she says, adding that listening to the experiences of victims “has been really impactful to me, and has helped me break the habit of being an advocate for one side.”  
Hearing cases involving litigants who represent themselves is challenging, Schwartz says. 
“I don’t attempt to give them advice on how to proceed or how to act, but I try to explain in layman’s terms, versus legal speak, what’s going on,” she says. 
If a pro se litigant fails to file a timely response to a motion, Schwartz says she’ll leave it on calendar in the event they appear and wish to orally state their case. 
Of the 177 attorneys responding to the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 evaluation, 75.5% said Schwartz should be retained. 
Her criminal case rulings were found to be in error in seven of 36 appeals, according to Our Nevada Judges. She has been appealed in three civil cases and was upheld in all. 
“I receive notices of appeal, but I don’t really pay attention,” says Schwartz. “My understanding is that my civil appeal rate is incredibly low. In criminal cases, anytime there’s a guilty verdict, there is automatically going to be an appeal.”
Schwartz is endorsed by Veterans in Politics. Her campaign expense report says she paid Veterans in Politics International $600 for consulting expenses.
Steve Sanson of VIPI says his company is not a consultant to Schwartz. He says the judge purchased advertising from VIP and recorded it incorrectly on her expense report. He says buying advertising does not guarantee an endorsement from the group.
Schwartz did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Other endorsements include more than a dozen law enforcement associations, the Nevada Veterans Association, Asian American Group, Professional Firefighters of Nevada, Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, SEIU Nevada, Culinary Local 226, and Teamsters Nevada, Independent Black Voters, and the National Organization for Women (NOW).
Schwartz had raised $274,000 and had about $210,000 in the bank as of July. 
Villani is also a graduate of Boyd School of Law. He is no relation to former Judge Michael Villani.
He did not respond to requests for an interview and has no current campaign website.
This is his second bid for the bench. In 2020 he lost the race for Dept. 1 by double digits to Bita Yeager.  
As of July he had received no campaign contributions. It’s unknown if he has any endorsements. 
Early voting begins Saturday, October 17.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri nonprofit launches campaign focused on abortion options ahead of November vote
description: As Missourians prepare to vote on whether to reinstate an abortion ban, a new information campaign by a local abortion fund is setting out to remind Missourians that regardless of what happens in November, some abortion options will remain available. The campaign launched last week and will run through Election Day, when Missourians will decide […]
text:
A billboard campaign by Missouri Abortion Fund and Shout Your Abortion is part of an effort to raise awareness around telehealth medication abortion access ahead of the November vote on abortion. One of the billboards is located off Interstate 70 in St. Louis (photo provided by STL From Above).As Missourians prepare to vote on whether to reinstate an abortion ban, a new information campaign by a local abortion fund is setting out to remind Missourians that regardless of what happens in November, some abortion options will remain available.
The campaign launched last week and will run through Election Day, when Missourians will decide whether to  repeal the 2024 reproductive rights amendment that legalized abortion up to the point of fetal viability.
The campaign, which includes billboards on the interstate heading into St. Louis and Kansas City, as well as video ads and mailers, comes amid continued statewide access fights and growing efforts nationally to restrict medication abortion.
“Our patients that we help, they can’t wait for policy changes, they can’t wait for elections. They need help today,” said Robin Frisella, communications director at Missouri Abortion Fund, a nonprofit that helps people pay for abortions. “There’s a real information and resource gap, and people are really left trying to figure out on their own what is actually legal.” 
Missouri Abortion Fund partnered with a Seattle nonprofit called Shout Your Abortion that provides information about abortion access, including obtaining medication abortion in advance.
The idea is to allow people to obtain abortion pills before facing an unplanned pregnancy so they already have the medication if they need it later.
“In the same way that I have Narcan in my bathroom cabinet even though I’m not an opioid user,” said Amelia Bonow, executive director of Shout Your Abortion. “SYA would love to help illustrate a future where people know that pills are available by mail in all 50 states.” 
After launching the first campaign in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, Bonow said they wanted to partner with organizations in states with more hostile abortion politics: Missouri and West Virginia.
“It’s clear that Missouri is a very uniquely-fraught state in terms of the information landscape,” Bonow said, pointing to the “strong, persistent presence” of the state’s anti-abortion movement.
Six months after Missourians narrowly approved the 2024 citizen-led reproductive freedom amendment, Republican lawmakers voted to place an abortion ban on the ballot. That proposed ban, which will appear on the ballot as Amendment 3, would outlaw nearly all abortions, with limited exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and survivors of rape or incest in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. 
The proposed amendment would also place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors, which is already outlawed in state statute. 
In the nearly two years since Missourians overturned the state’s near-total abortion ban, the state’s Planned Parenthood clinics have gradually resumed medication and procedural abortions while courts considered challenges to regulations enacted before the constitutional amendment.
Ongoing federal efforts to limit or ban mifepristone access are led by U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
“It’s clear that misinformation, disinformation, people simply not knowing what their options are is one of the biggest problems there,” Bonow said.
The November vote is only one source of uncertainty surrounding abortion access. Another is the growing political and legal fight over abortion pills obtained through telehealth.
Under federal law, women in every state, regardless of abortion legality, can order medication abortion to their home by seeking a prescription from an out-of-state provider. 
But for several Republican leaders at the national level, including U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, efforts to limit or eliminate access to mifepristone are a top priority. 
Hawley in recent months has urged the Justice Department to investigate mifepristone’s manufacturer, launched a national political group aimed at reshaping abortion debates, asked the FDA to review the safety and efficacy of mifepristone, and has introduced legislation to withdraw FDA approval of the medication.
“The time for bold leadership is now,” Hawley said at the Pray, Vote, Stand summit hosted last week by the Family Research Council. “There is a role for Congress, and it is to ban mifepristone.” 
Medication abortions obtained through telehealth have become increasingly common, including among patients living in states with abortion bans and restrictions.
Between 2023 and 2025, the number of Missourians who obtained medication abortions through telehealth from out-of-state clinicians nearly quadrupled, from about 880 to 3,220, according to data released by the Guttmacher Institute. Nationwide, medication abortion now accounts for about two-thirds of abortions.
That access has also emerged as a fault line among abortion opponents in the campaign over Amendment 3. Some anti-abortion activists and lawmakers argue the proposed ban isn’t strict enough, and that the threat of criminalization is the only way to reduce abortions.
Anti-abortion divide could complicate Missouri Amendment 3 campaign

Mifepristone is typically used with misoprostol for medication abortions. Mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed for a pregnancy to continue. Misoprostol causes the uterus to contract and empty. The medications are also used in miscarriage care.
Bleeding and cramping are expected side effects. Serious complications, including heavy bleeding and infection, are rare.
Even when abortion is legally available, cost can remain a barrier because insurance coverage is limited. Groups such as Missouri Abortion Fund help patients cover those expenses. But Frisella said the organization has seen its pool of donors shrink.
Ballot campaigns, like the Stop the Ban effort to vote down Amendment 3, can attract donors who might otherwise give directly to groups helping patients pay for abortions, Frisella said.
As a result, Frisella said, Missouri Abortion Fund has seen a heavy decline in sustained monthly donors. Right now, the nonprofit gives about $45,000 a month toward helping Missourians pay for abortions. That funding usually runs out by the middle of the month, she said. 
Many of those patients are still traveling to Kansas or Illinois for abortion access as Missouri clinics work to rebuild an infrastructure decimated by years of abortion regulations, restrictions and lawsuits. 
In July, for example, Missouri Abortion Fund helped 80 patients afford abortions, Frisella said. Only 12 were seen in Missouri; the rest went to Kansas and Illinois. 
Missourians are used to a constantly changing abortion landscape, Frisella said. But it doesn’t make the current state of access any less confusing. She still receives emails from women asking if they can access abortion in Missouri, and if they’re legally allowed to leave the state to access it elsewhere. 
“There’s a real information and resource gap,” Frisella said. “And people are really left trying to figure out on their own what is actually legal.”
Bonow, like Frisella, is looking beyond November. 
“Policy is insufficient to address the crisis of abortion access,” she said, calling abortion funds “the foundation of abortion access in this country, not a ballot measure that will ping and pong back and forth a million different times.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The false savings — and cruelty — of cutting GLP-1 coverage in Massachusetts
description: Ending coverage does not merely stop progress. It reverses it—and costs may return as diabetes, CPAP equipment, additional medications, disability, and hospital care.
text:
I AM PROTECTED by a diagnosis. 
After I began taking a GLP-1–based medication, my A1C fell from 12 to 6 within months. Because I have type 2 diabetes, my insurance continues to cover the drug. Patients receiving medications from the same class to treat obesity may not have that protection—even when treatment is producing measurable health improvements. 
Thousands of Massachusetts residents now face losing access. This summer, MassHealth, the state Medicaid program that insures low-income residents, ended coverage for medications prescribed solely to treat obesity, affecting approximately 22,000 members. The state’s Group Insurance Commission, which oversees coverage for public employees, has done the same, a move that affects about the same number of people. Private insurers across the Commonwealth have also restricted obesity coverage while generally preserving it for diabetes. 
Nothing about these medications’ effectiveness changed. What changed was who would pay for them—and therefore who could continue receiving them. 
The United States spends more per person on health care than other wealthy countries without achieving correspondingly better outcomes. Yet Massachusetts insurers are withdrawing coverage for a medication class that produces measurable health improvements. 
These medications do far more than change how people look. They can improve blood sugar, cardiovascular risk factors, sleep apnea, and mobility. The Food and Drug Administration approved the GLP-1 drug Zepbound to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity after clinical trials demonstrated meaningful improvement. In a separate large trial, another GLP-1 medication, semaglutide, reduced major cardiovascular events by 20 percent among adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease who did not have diabetes. 
These are the outcomes our expensive health care system should be trying to achieve. 
Insurers and state officials face a real affordability problem. These medications remain expensive, many patients could qualify, and treatment may be needed long term. Massachusetts insurers have cited coverage restrictions among factors contributing to stronger financial results in 2026. Point32Health estimated that its restrictions could save $100 million or more this year. 
As a CPA, I understand why those figures command attention. As a nurse, I question a calculation that recognizes the immediate cost of treatment more readily than the future cost of disease. 
The reductions may save insurers money, but Massachusetts consumers should not expect meaningful premium relief. State regulators have approved an average 10.4 percent premium increase for 2027 in the individual and small-group market. 
Patients are losing treatment. Insurers are recording savings. Premiums are still increasing. What health care outcome is this strategy designed to achieve? 
When coverage forces treatment to stop, the consequences are predictable. One year after semaglutide treatment ended, trial participants had regained two-thirds of the weight they had lost, while most improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, and other cardiometabolic measures moved back toward baseline. In a trial of the GLP-1 drug tirzepatide, participants who were switched to placebo regained an average of 14 percent of their body weight during the following year, while those who continued treatment lost another 5.5 percent. 
Ending coverage does not merely stop progress. It reverses it—and costs may return as diabetes, CPAP equipment, additional medications, disability, and hospital care. 
The insurer paying for treatment today may not cover those consequences years from now. Patients change jobs, health plans, and eligibility. One organization can capture immediate savings while another payer—or the patient—absorbs the later cost. That is cost transfer, not necessarily cost reduction. 
It also risks deepening inequality. Nearly 1 million Massachusetts residents rely on SNAP to help afford food. For households already balancing food, housing, utilities, and medical expenses, another three-figure monthly bill for a costly medication may be impossible. Continued treatment becomes increasingly dependent on who can afford it. 
Massachusetts should confront excessive drug prices directly by negotiating lower prices, using evidence-based eligibility requirements, and preserving coverage for patients demonstrating meaningful improvement. It should not force patients to regain weight or develop diabetes before treatment becomes worthy of coverage. 
Massachusetts regulators should also require health plans that restrict coverage to report how many patients lose treatment, what happens to their health afterward, and whether projected pharmacy savings are offset by higher medical spending elsewhere. Without that accounting, the Commonwealth cannot know whether it is controlling health care costs or simply shifting them to patients, families, and future payers. 
My diagnosis protects my access to a medication class that transformed my health. I am grateful. But I cannot accept a system that offers another patient less protection because treatment worked before diabetes developed—or because that patient cannot afford to purchase better health privately. 
In a state known for health care innovation, saving insurers money should not be mistaken for improving health. Massachusetts should demand both affordability and access. 
Courtney Desy is an oncology nurse and CPA.

name: Nevada Current
title: Henderson councilwoman faces election challenge amid ongoing felony case
description: Henderson City Councilwoman Carrie Cox, who among a flurry of scandals is facing a criminal investigation, is at risk of being unseated this November by Jennifer Atlas, a nonprofit government affairs director. Cox, who has represented Ward 3 since 2022, was indicted last year on a felony charge for monitoring or attempting to monitor a […]
text:
Jennifer Atlas, Carrie Cox. (Candidate photos)Henderson City Councilwoman Carrie Cox, who among a flurry of scandals is facing a criminal investigation, is at risk of being unseated this November by Jennifer Atlas, a nonprofit government affairs director.
Cox, who has represented Ward 3 since 2022, was indicted last year on a felony charge for monitoring or attempting to monitor a private conversation. The category D felony could carry a 1-to-4-year sentence. 
She pleaded not guilty. She previously told Nevada Current she maintains her innocence and “the truth will come out,” adding that, “People will be shocked by the lies.” 
Her attorney filed a motion last month seeking to postpone the trial currently set for later this month. A judge is scheduled to hold a hearing Oct. 6 to decide if the trial will proceed. 
In an interview with The Nevada Independent, Atlas said it was unacceptable that Cox is still representing the ward.
Atlas, one of three candidates who ran against Cox in June, received 38% or nearly 4,400 votes during the primary. Cox came in second and received roughly 31% or 3,500 votes. 
Since no candidate received a majority of the vote, the top two finishers advanced to the general election. 
Cox first ran for city council in 2017 against Ward 3 incumbent Councilman John Marz but lost by nearly three points – she received 6,675 votes to his 7,115 in an off-year election cycle. 
She ran again during the 2022 midterm election, coming in second in the primary but winning in the general election by three points. 
Cox was charged in November 2025 for allegedly hiding behind a curtain at City Hall and recording her colleague in a conversation with constituents.
“Investigators found Cox surreptitiously recorded many encounters with various people,” the police investigation reads, adding it’s “important to note that while surreptitiously recording in-person conversations, in which an individual is a part of, is not illegal” but suggests “it does however reveal a pattern of conduct.”
Following the indictment, the Henderson City Council voted unanimously to censure Cox and filed a complaint against her at the Nevada Commission on Ethics. 
This year, the commission dismissed the complaint, saying “the facts do not establish credible evidence to support a determination that just and sufficient cause exists for the Commission to render an opinion in this matter.” 
The commission issued a letter warning Cox that her conduct implicated ethics law and to provide guidance on future compliance.  
But it isn’t the only scandal plaguing Cox ahead of the election. 
Most recently, the Nevada Association of Public Safety Officers and the Henderson Police Supervisors Association sent a cease-and-desist letter to Cox in August telling her to stop using their “names, badges, logos, and other identifying information” in her campaign ads, saying her signs are false and misleading.
“Your re-election campaign has NOT been endorsed by either Association,” the letter reads. “Furthermore, both Association previously rescinded old endorsements. Indicating that you have our local police endorsement is FALSE and represents a factual misrepresentation to the community.” 
The Nevada Association of Public Safety Officers and Henderson Police Supervisors Association have endorsed Atlas, as have the AFL-CIO, Culinary Union, SEIU, and Teamsters Nevada.
Atlas currently works for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network. A Democrat, she challenged incumbent Republican state Sen. Carrie Buck in 2024 but lost by seven points. 
Prior to her entrance into the political sphere, Atlas was a competitive ballroom dancer and teacher as well as a convention gig and concierge worker. 
Like in campaigns across the state, and country alike, Atlas has said affordability is the top concern of residents saying on her campaign website that “city government can do more to help businesses grow, add jobs and diversify our economy.” 
She previously told the Current she would like to see Henderson “put up some guardrails” to limit corporate homebuying.
While it is a nonpartisan race, Cox is endorsed by the Clark County Republican Party. 
Though she hasn’t raised much in the most recent campaign finance reporting cycle, Cox still surpasses Atlas in total campaign dollars on hand. 
Atlas had $11,236 on hand while Cox had $99,353 on hand as of July 1, according to campaign finance reports.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: I’m voting early and you should, too
description: Election Day is not for another month, but you should get your vote in now if you can. Mail in your ballots ASAP or make a plan to vote in person starting Oct. 24.
text:
Election Day is not for another month, but you should get your vote in now if you can. Mail in your ballots ASAP or make a plan to vote in person starting Oct. 24. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]There are still 32 days until Election Day, but my advice to voters who have mail-in ballots is to cast them now.
Yes, the U.S. Supreme Court has halted a Trump administration push to revamp mail-in voting that one whistleblower alleged would have created chaos and led to untold numbers of disenfranchised voters. But the president is still intent on curbing this method of voting, and who knows what he’ll direct the U.S. Postal Service to do as it gets closer to Election Day. So if you have a mail-in ballot, fill it out and cast it today.
Some anxious Democrats are urging their voters to skip the post office altogether. Mercer County’s clerk sent a mailer to voters urging them to use ballot dropboxes instead, and Democrats in Maplewood have issued a similar warning.
I had intended to make the same plea. Dan Bryan, a Democratic political operative, said I was being a bit of a worrywart and cautioned that such warnings this far out from Election Day are irresponsible.
“I think there is no evidence that between now and let’s call it a few days before Election Day anyone has anything to worry about putting their ballot in the mail,” Bryan said.
Putting a mail-in ballot in a dropbox is more foolproof, he conceded, because that avoids the post office middleman altogether, but it also adds an additional barrier for voters with busy lives. Looking up the location of and driving to a dropbox is a few steps harder than sticking a stamp on a ballot and leaving it in your own mailbox, he said.
One of the reasons vote-by-mail is so effective, he said, is “because it’s really f***ing easy.”
That’s fair, but I would say this particular errand is so important, even the busiest among us should find the time to do it and avoid any possibility of the Postal Service screwing with your vote. You can find our local dropbox here.
I do not think this is an area where only Democrats should be concerned, though obviously the president’s mission here is to help the GOP.
The unnamed whistleblower alleges the Postal Service had planned to create a new online portal to screen ballots submitted by election officials prior to them being mailed to voters. If a single ballot in a large batch could not be verified — even if the problem was, say, a recently married woman whose last name has changed — then the entire batch of ballots would be rejected, the whistleblower alleged. A voter expecting a mail-in ballot may not even know that ballot was rejected until it’s too late to request a new one.
I live in Bloomfield, where 67% of voters cast ballots for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024. But 7,308 of my neighbors voted for Trump. It is implausible to believe that a rejection of a large batch of mail-in ballots by our post office wouldn’t also result in some Republican voters not getting their ballots.
I myself will vote in person because I’m a Gen X-er who still pays for cable TV and has a working iPod; I prefer to cast my ballot the old-fashioned way. But I don’t plan to wait until Election Day. Early in-person voting in New Jersey starts Oct. 24. I’m voting early and you should, too.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Fiery crowd caps redistricting hearings. Opponents urge: ‘Leave our maps alone’
description: Participants march to the Capitol after the ACLU of Mississippi’s voting rights rally in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Tempers flared Thursday at a packed redistricting hearing at the Mississippi Capitol, where a large majority of speakers criticized what they said was a power grab aimed at diminishing Black political power and further entrenching Republican dominance over state politics. 
The hearing in Jackson capped off a slate of often fiery public hearings that began in August, and included stops in north Mississippi, the Delta, east Mississippi and the Gulf Coast. A Republican-dominated committee listened to speakers who shared their views on whether Mississippi should redraw its electoral maps, a move that could reshape the state’s political representation for years to come. 
Republicans control the state Legislature and currently hold three out of the state’s four seats in the U.S. House, but they could potentially redraw maps to further strengthen their grip on Mississippi’s political offices.  
Mississippians arrived at the Capitol Thursday wielding placards, megaphones and shirts emblazoned with the phrase “I FIGHT FOR VOTING RIGHTS.” A smattering of pro-redistricting attendees wearing signature red blazers of the Mississippi Federation of Republican Women were sitting in the front row, but opponents of redistricting dominated the crowd. 

Many speakers pointed out the state’s sordid history of racial discrimination, and the committee’s composition reflected the intertwined nature of racial and political polarization in Mississippi. The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, consists of 16 Republicans, all but one of whom are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. 
Walter Boone, a Jackson resident, urged lawmakers not to further continue a historical pattern of policymaking that harms Black residents, and sign their names to what he called “the Mississippi Plan 2.0.”
